H8_Notes: This is a continuation of the existing policy commenced in April. The national government agreed that visits in aged care facilities should be limited to a short duration, a maximum of two visitors at one time per day, and conducted in line with social distancing practices. Infection prevention and control measures must be balanced against the needs and best interests of residents. Aged care providers are best placed to make these assessments on a case by case basis. The following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter the aged care facilities: â€¢ Those who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days; â€¢ Those who have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days; â€¢ Those with fever or any (even mild) symptoms of acute respiratory infection (e.g. cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath); and â€¢ Those who have not been vaccinated against influenza (after 1 May). The national government stressed that it is not acceptable for any facility to put in place restrictions beyond the principles agreed. These include complete lockdowns or banning all visits from carers and families, other than during a specified facility outbreak. Facilities need to know the appropriate levels of infection control and prevention to implement, in consultation with the relevant public health units and the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission. The Commonwealth Government will continue to monitor the situation and will take steps, if necessary, to require facilities to seek an exemption from the Commission before implementing additional restrictions. Additionally, on 1 May, the Morrison government announces the additional covid-19 specific support packaging totalling $205 million under targeted measures. The support is aimed at ensuring aged care providers can offer reinforced levels of safety and care for those who need it most. Endorsement of â€˜Code of Conduct on Pandemic Proceduresâ€™ draft for residential aged care is made by the National cabinet in order to drive a more responsive and consistent approach to visitation and communication across residential aged care. https://web.archive.org/web/20220512035907/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/new-covid-19-payment-keep-senior-australians-residential-aged-care-safe https://web.archive.org/web/20220512034531/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures-1may20 https://web.archive.org/web/20220515000647/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures-24april20     Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20220515000643/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures-210420

C1_Notes: According to the NSW Government (updated on 12 June 2020), schools in NSW are operating full time, and many additional activities are now able to recommence. All schools have returned to full-time on-campus learning. Students do not need to follow strict adult physical distancing guidelines, but should follow good hygiene practices like:  -regularly washing hands  -avoiding sharing drinks or food  -coughing or sneezing into your elbow, or a tissue which should be discarded immediately  -filling water bottles from bubblers rather than using the bubbler directly.    Additionally, the physical distancing of children in schools is not required under the Australian HPPC guidelines. Research has shown limited transmission risk associated with school children in the school environment. All adults must maintain physical distance from each other (1.5m) including teachers and support staff, and parents.    Schools will continue to receive additional cleaning in line with the AHPPC guidelines and advice from NSW Health. Target areas include high-touch areas and other hard surfaces, door handles, lockers, light switches and handrails in stairways and movement areas. There will also be additional cleaning of toilets and bubblers and topping up of supplies like soap.    This represents a continuation of the policy of significant changes to pre-covid times. C4_Notes: According to the NSW Government (updated on 1 July 2020), no more than 20 people are allowed to gather outside in a public place.    Different gatherings have different levels of restrictions. Since the OxCGRT reports the stricter policy, in this case, 20 people should be reported.    This represents a continuation of the policy of significant changes to pre-covid times.    Notes:  For visiting family and friends at home, up to 20 visitors may visit another household at any one time. The total number of visitors includes adults and children.    For outdoor public gatherings, no more than 20 people are allowed to gather outside in a public place.    For funerals, memorial services and wakes, the maximum number of people who may attend a funeral is the maximum number of people allowed on the premises, which is one person per 4 square metres. Places of public worship, funeral homes or crematoriums can have up to 50 attendees (without the 4 square metre rule) provided non-household contacts can maintain 1.5 metres of physical distance. Funerals at a place of residence can have the greater of 50 people or one person per 4 square metres of space.    For religious gatherings and places of worship, the number of people in a public place of worship must not exceed one person per 4 square metres. The maximum applies to the whole of the venue, even where men and women worship in separate areas.    For weddings, the maximum number of people who may attend a wedding is the maximum number of people allowed on the premises, which is one person per 4 square metres. Wedding services are no longer subject to separate limits, with the exception of a wedding at a place of residence, which can have the greater of 20 people or one person per 4 square metres of space. C1_Notes: As of the last update on 8 December 2020, according to the New South Wales (NSW) Department of Education, there are significant changes to school operation when compared to pre-COVID-19. This includes significant cleaning measures (NSW government providing cleaning supplies and additional cleaning schedules), teachers, staff and parents requiring to physically distance and COVID Safe plans for school events. Nonetheless, when compared to the previous restrictions, this updated policy represents a relaxation in the school restrictions.    As of 19 December 2020, the Northern Beaches area entered lockdown. There are only four reasons people are permitted to leave the house, education is one of them. C2_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 19/12/2020, all residents of the Northern Beaches Local Government Area are required to work at home where this is possible, with this policy in effect from 5pm on 19/12/2020 until 11.59pm on 23/12/2020.    A number of workplaces on the Northern Beaches are required to close, including indoor recreation facilities, places of public worship, beauty businesses, sex services premises. Pubs and food and drink premises must close except for the purpose of selling takeaway food or beverages.     This tightening of restrictions is in response to the development of community spread in the area.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210415072934/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increase-covid-19-cases-northern-beaches-area  http://web.archive.org/web/20220310012632/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20%28COVID-19%20Northern%20Beaches%29%20Order%202020.pdf
C3_Notes: As announced by Gladys Berejiklian on 19/12/2020, a stay-at-home order is in place for the Northern Beaches until 11.59pm 23/12/2020, meaning all public events here must be cancelled.     Residents across Greater Sydney are also urged to limit unnecessary activitity.    This tightening of restrictions is in response to the development of community spread on the Northern Beaches.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210415072934/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increase-covid-19-cases-northern-beaches-area
C4_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 19/12/2020, a stay-at-home order is being put into place on the Northern Beaches until 23/12/2020. As a result, all gatherings outside the house in this area are banned.     This tightening of restrictions is in response to the development of community spread in this area.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210415072934/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increase-covid-19-cases-northern-beaches-area
C6_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 19/12/2020, a stay-at-home order is being put into place on the Northern Beaches from 11.59PM 19/12/2020 until 11.59PM 23/12/2020.    All residents in this area must remain at home unless they are leaving for an essential reason, of which there are four:    - Shopping for good or others goods and services  - Medical care or compassionate needs  - Exercise  - Work or education, where you cannot work at home.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210415072934/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increase-covid-19-cases-northern-beaches-area
C7_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 19/12/2020, a number of restrictions on internal movement are being put in force until 23/12/2020. Persons are not permitted to enter the Northern Beaches unless they have a reasonable excuse, which includes:    - Entering to travel to a place of residence.  - Travelling through the area without leaving the vehicle.  - Attending a funeral with less than 100 persons or a wedding on 20/12/2020.  - Entering for a variety of essential reasons, not including to exercise or donate blood.    This tightening of restrictions is a response to the development of community spread in the Northern Beaches.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210415072934/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increase-covid-19-cases-northern-beaches-area  http://web.archive.org/web/20220310012632/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20%28COVID-19%20Northern%20Beaches%29%20Order%202020.pdf

C3_Notes: As announced by Gladys Berejiklian on 20/12/2020, a number of restrictions are being implemented in Greater Sydney, including some which affect public events. A one person per four square metre density limit is reintroduced for all indoor settings, and a cap of 300 people applies to hospitality venues and places of worship. Singing and chanting at indoor venues is not allowed, and dancefloors are only permitted at wedding with a maximum of 20 people.     This amounts to a recommended cancellation of public events, but the stricter policy that remains in place in the Northern Beaches is recorded.    http://web.archive.org/web/20210401154042/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/new-covid-19-restrictions-for-greater-sydney
C4_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 20/12/2020, restrictions on gatherings are being implemented in Greater Sydney as of 11.59PM 20/12/2020, until 11.59PM 23/12/2020. Household gatherings are limited to 10 visitors, which would be coded as 3, but the stricter restrictions are in the Northern Beaches are instead recorded.    This tightening of restrictions is an effort to prevent community spread occuring across Greater Sydney.    http://web.archive.org/web/20210401154042/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/new-covid-19-restrictions-for-greater-sydney

C2_Notes: As announced by Gladys Berejiklian on 23/12/2020, the restrictions on workplaces announced on 19/12/2020 will now extend to 26/12/2020. This requires all people on the Northern Beaches to work from home, and closes a number of types of premises.    http://web.archive.org/web/20220309110546/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C3_Notes: As announced by Gladys Berejiklian on 23/12/2020, restrictions on public events in the Northern Beaches and Greater Sydney will remain in place until 26/12/2020. This requires all events on the Northern Beaches to be cancelled, and imposes density and attendance limits on events in Greater Sydney.    http://web.archive.org/web/20220309110546/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C4_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 23/12/2020, restrictions on gatherings in the Northern Beaches and the Greater Sydney Area are being modified and extended until 26/12/2020.    In the northern zone of the Northern Beaches, residents are able to visit the homes of others in this area, with a maximum of 5 visitors including Children.    In the southern zone of the Northern Beaches, residents are allowed to up to 10 visitors in their home, plus primary school aged children and younger. These visitors must not come from the northern zone, but can include residents of either the southern zone or the rest of Greater Sydney.    In the Greater Sydney region,  the restriction on household gatherings to 10 visitor remains, but primary school-aged children and younger are no longer counted in this cap.     This small loosening in restrictions intends to balance the social desire of contact during the Christmas period and concerns about community transmission.    http://web.archive.org/web/20220309110546/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C6_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 23/12/2020, the stay-at-home order in the Northern Beaches is being extended until 26/12/2020 with some modifications, including the division of the area into two separate northern and southern zones.     In both zones, an additional reason to leave the home has been added - to visit the home of others within ones zone. These indoor gatherings are limited to 5 visitors in the northern zone, and 10 visitors in the southern zone.     This loosening in restrictions is an attempt to balance social contact during the Christmas with the risk of community spread.    http://web.archive.org/web/20220309110546/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C7_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 23/12/2020, previous restrictions on internal movement are being extended until 26/12/2020, with one modification. Visitors from outside the Northern Beaches are allowed to enter to visit the homes of people within the southern zone.    Otherwise, the restrictions on entry or exit of the Northern Beaches to essential purposes remains in place.    http://web.archive.org/web/20220309110546/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period

C2_Notes: As announced by Gladys Berejiklian on 26/12/2020, existing restrictions on workplaces in the Northern Beaches will remain in place until 30/12/2020. This requires all people in this area to work from home and closes a number of types of premises.    Additionally, those who work in Sydney CBD are urged to work for home where practical.  http://web.archive.org/web/20210401185021/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/update-on-restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C3_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 26/12/2020, previous restrictions in place on public events will be extended until 11.59 30/12/2020. This involves the cancellation of all public events in the Northern Beaches, and density and attendance limits in other areas of Greater Sydney.    This continuation of restrictions is in response to the ongoing risk of community spread.    http://web.archive.org/web/20210401185021/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/update-on-restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C4_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 26/12/2020, restrictions on gatherings in the Northern Beaches and Greater Sydney Area are being strengthened and extended until 30/12/2020.    In the northern zone of the Northern Beaches, indoor gatherings are no longer allowed. Outdoor gatherings of 5 people, including children, are allowed for exercise or recreational activity.    In the southern zone of the Northern Beaches, indoors gatherings are also no longer allowed. Outdoor gatherings of 10 people from within this zone are allowed for exerercise or recreational activity.    Restrictions are tightened for the rest of the Greater Sydney area, with indoor gatherings limited to 10 people per household, including visitors and residents.    http://web.archive.org/web/20210401185021/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/update-on-restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C6_Notes: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 26/12/2020, the stay-at-home order in the Northern Beaches is being extended until 30/12/2020 and restrictions tightened.    Residents in both zones are no longer permitted to leave their home to visit others in their zone. However, outdoor gatherings within ones zone for the purpose of exercise or recreational activity are now allowed. In the northern zone, up to 5 people including children may gather. In the southern zone, up to 10 people including children may gather.    This tightening of restrictions is a response to health advice on the risk of community spread in indoor areas.    http://web.archive.org/web/20210401185021/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/update-on-restrictions-for-christmas-2020-period
C7_Notes: As detailed by Minister for Health and Medical Research Brad Hazzard, additional restrictions on internal movement were put into effect on 29/12/2020. C4_Notes: There were some minor regional variations in NSW Government policy, but these generally did not trigger changes in the ordinal coding scale:    According to an announcement made on 21 September 2021 on the NSW Health website, children aged 18 years old in parts of NSW under stay at home orders would be allowed to create 'friends bubbles' from noon on 21 September 2021. Friends bubbles were subject to the following conditions:  	- Everyone in a friends bubble had to live in the same LGA or within 5 kilometres of each other  	- Everyone aged 18+ in each participating household was required to be fully vaccinated or have a medical exemption  	- Parents and carers dropping their children off at friends' houses were not allowed to interact with other parents  	- The members of a friends bubble must stay the same, and each child could only be part of one friends bubble.    Other gathering restrictions remained the same:    In parts of NSW under stay at home orders (some regional LGAs, Greater Sydney, and LGAs of concern), up to 5 fully vaccinated or 2 unvaccinated individuals aged 16 years old or above could gather together for outdoor recreation. Individuals were not permitted to accept visitors (other than nominated visitors or people in their friends bubble) unless there was an essential reason to do so (e.g. for necessary childcare arrangements, permitted work, or compassionate reasons).    In some regional NSW LGAs which were no longer under stay at home orders, up to 5 visitors were allowed in a home regardless of vaccination status. The maximum number of people permitted at outdoor events was as follows:  	a) For major recreation outdoor facilities - 5000 people  	b) For controlled outdoor public gatherings - 500 people  	c) For COVID-19 safe outdoor public gatherings - 50 people  	d) For all other outdoor gatherings - 20 people. E1_Notes: People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. As of 1 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments

H8_Notes: The following restrictions were a continuation of existing policy and applied to the whole of NSW.  According to the NSW Health website as of 30 November 2021, individuals were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had COVID-19 symptoms, were close or casual contacts of COVID-19 cases who had not completed self-isolation and testing requirements, were waiting for a COVID-19 test result, or had not fulfilled testing and vaccination requirements if they had been overseas in the past 14 days. C4_Notes: The following restrictions were a continuation of existing policy and applied to the whole of NSW. Different restrictions were in place for vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals.    According to the NSW Government website as of 6 December 2021 and the Public Health (COVID-19 General) Order 2021 (as in force between 10 November and 15 December 2021), individuals who were not fully vaccinated were prohibited from visiting others at their places of residences except for caring and compassionate reasons. Additionally, they could only attend outdoor gatherings with up to one other person outside their household. Unvaccinated individuals were  prohibited from attending a wide range of nonessential venues, such as high risk venues, personal care services, indoor recreational facilities, retail (except for essential retail), as well as information and education facilities. Wedding with unvaccinated adults present were allowed to have a maximum of 11 attendees, and funerals with unvaccinated adults present were allowed to have a maximum of 10 attendees.    Vaccinated individuals were allowed to visit venues, with some capacity and density restrictions in place. All premises (with some exceptions) were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metre density rule. Some ticketed and seated events could operate at 100% capacity, and commercial vessels could exceed 1 person per 2 square metres if they had fewer than 50 people on board. Indoor gym and dance classes were allowed to open with a maximum of 20 people per class.     All music festivals were prohibited.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211206054005/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/stay-safe/rules/not-fully-vaccinated  https://web.archive.org/web/20211206223018/https:/legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20General)%20Order%202021_211110.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20220818201455/https:/legislation.nsw.gov.au/information/covid19-legislation/general  https://web.archive.org/web/20211207053616/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/public-health-orders.aspx#gatherings

C7_Notes: According to the NSW Government website (as of 13 December 2021), the NSW Health website (as of 9 and 15 December 2021), and the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice (as approved on 13 December 2021) the following restrictions were largely a continuation of existing restrictions and applied to the whole of NSW, although some restrictions placed on unvaccinated individuals were lifted on 15 December 2021.    Unvaccinated individuals in NSW were prohibited from going on holidays or recreation outside their LGA. All unvaccinated residents of Victoria above the age of 16 were prohibited from travelling to NSW for holiday or recreation purposes.  According to the Public Health (COVID-19 General) Order (No 2) 2021, which came into effect on 15 December 2021, these restrictions were lifted on 15 December 2021.    Vaccinated individuals did not face any restrictions on travel within NSW.    Some locations in the ACT, Queensland, and Victoria were listed as places of high concern, and individuals who had visited these places were required to follow travel restrictions when entering NSW:    Close contacts of COVID-19 cases who had been to places of high concern interstate (as listed in the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice) and were not NSW residents were prohibited from entering NSW if they were not fully vaccinated. Vaccinated close contacts entering NSW were required to self-isolate until it had been at least 7 days after they had last visited a place of high concern.    Casual contacts of COVID-19 cases who had been to places of high concern interstate (as listed in the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice) and were not NSW residents were allowed to enter NSW as long as they had returned a negative COVID-19 test result and completed a travel declaration within 24 hours of entry*.    NSW residents entering NSW who were close contacts of COVID-19 cases that had been to places of high concern interstate (as listed in the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice) were required to self-isolate for 7 days (or 14 days if not fully vaccinated) until they had last visited the place of high concern.  NSW residents entering NSW who were casual contacts of COVID-19 cases that had been to places of high concern interstate (as listed in the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice) were required to self-isolate until they returned a negative COVID-19 test result.    *The interstate travel rules webpage also stated that travel declarations were no longer necessary, so it is unclear what travellers needed to complete these.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211213214641/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/travel-restrictions/interstate-travel-rules  https://web.archive.org/web/20211209002335/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/public-health-orders.aspx#interstate  https://web.archive.org/web/20211214200616/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/public-health-orders.aspx#interstate  https://web.archive.org/web/20211213214635/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Documents/interstate-concerns-notice.pdf    Links to formal legislation for the general NSW area:  The Public Health (COVID-19 General) Order 2021 (in place from 10/11/2021 - 15/12/2021) contained directions prohibiting unvaccinated adults from undertaking recreation outside their LGA, and unvaccinated Victorians from entering NSW for recreation.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211206223018/https:/legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20General)%20Order%202021_211110.pdf  The Public Health (COVID-19 General) Order (No 2) 2021, which came into effect on 15 December 2021, contained no mention of the above restrictions.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211216060508/https:/legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20General)%20Order%20(No%202)%202021.pdf    https://web.archive.org/web/20220818201455/https:/legislation.nsw.gov.au/information/covid19-legislation/general

E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. H7_Notes: According to the Australian Government Department of Health website (as last updated 3 February 2022), the Australian Government had been distributing COVID-19 vaccines through Operation COVID Shield, the national taskforce coordinating the Australian vaccine rollout.    As part of the rollout, all Australians* aged 5 years and over could book a free COVID-19 vaccination appointment, although it was slightly more difficult for those in the 5-11 year age group to receive a vaccine compared to other eligible age groups, as not all vaccine providers were able to provide the smaller Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose for 5-11 year olds.    The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.    As 93.65% of Australians aged 16 years and above had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, 77.11% of Australians aged 12-15 years old had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, and 44.15% of Australians aged 5-11 years old had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, the Australian Government was likely able to deliver on its universal vaccination policy. Nonetheless, State and Territory Governments also delivered their own updates and specialised services to meet the needs of their jurisdictions. H8_Notes: "As published on 25 March 2022, there are some restrictions on visits to residential aged care facilities. 2 fully vaccinated visitors over the age of 12 are permitted per day  but the following requirements must be met:   - Visitors aged 12 years and over must have received a second dose of a COVID vaccination at least 14 days prior to their visit.  - Visitors are strongly encouraged to get a booster vaccine if they are eligible for one, and to have a negative Rapid Antigen Testing (RAT) prior to each visit  - Up to 2 children under 12 years are permitted to visit provided they are accompanied by a fully vaccinated person.  - All visitors must wear a surgical mask over their nose and mouth while visiting indoors. For reasons when masks can be removed please see Additional Advice â€“ Mandatory mask wearing.  - Wherever possible, the visit should be in an outdoor area. Visits should not be in any inside communal areas.  - People who are providing a service to the resident (including a health or other professional service) are not counted as a visitor.  - Existing requirements in the Public Health (COVID-19 Care Services) Order 2022 on visiting residents who are at end of life remain in place.  Non vaccinated visitors are allowed if they have an exemption:   An exemption to the Public Health (COVID-19 Care Services) Order 2022 has been signed to allow unvaccinated visitors to a resident who is at the end of life:  The exemption is subject to the condition that the operator of the facility takes reasonable steps to ensure:  - no more than 4 people (including children) visit at any one time  - all visitors wear a mask while in an indoor area, unless the visitor is interacting with the resident they are visiting  - there is minimal interaction between the visitors and the staff and other residents  - The visitors in this circumstance do not need to be vaccinated, however appropriate care must be taken if unvaccinated visitors are entering the facility. It is strongly recommended:  - the visit is solely inside the resident's room and  - the visitors perform a Rapid Antigen Testing (RAT) just before the visit.  Visitors cannot enter a facility if they have COVID-19, exposed to COVID-19, waiting for a test result or have been overseas in the previous 14 days and have not met the isolation requirements  This policy is in place across NSW and represents a continuance of the policy.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220409083148/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/racf-latest-advice.aspx  "

C1_Notes: As of 22 April 2022, there are updated COVID-19 policies in preparation for the new term. If someone in a student's household is discovered to have tested positive to COVID-19 in the last seven days, schools are now required to have all staff and secondary school students wear masks for the next five days while primary school students are suggested to do the same. All staff and students must also do a rapid antigen test (RAT) before school for the next five days. However, students that are household contacts are not required to self-isolate if no symptoms are displayed.    School-level outbreaks of COVID-19 may lead to the implementation of several temporary measures such as ceasing large indoor events, symptomatic use of RATs and limiting school visitors. Staff are still required to be vaccinated and students are strongly encouraged to. Schools are still recommended to use outdoor spaces for ventilation. This is a continuation of the previous policies from Term 1.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220429014643/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/stay-safe/advice-for-parents-students

As of 4 May, previous policies for schools remain relatively unchanged as Term 2 continues. As before, staff and secondary school students are only required to wear masks for the next five days if someone in a student's household is found infected while primary school students are suggested to do the same. All staff and students must also do a rapid antigen test (RAT) before school for the next five days. However, masks must be worn by any workers supporting students with disabilities in schools and close contact staff or high school students returning to school for the first five days and recommended for primary school students.    School-level outbreaks of COVID-19 may lead to the implementation of several temporary measures such as ceasing large indoor events, symptomatic use of RATs and limiting school visitors but cohosting is still relatively unrestricted. Staff are still required to be vaccinated and students are strongly encouraged to. Schools are still recommended to use outdoor spaces for ventilation or, with winter, having windows and doors slightly open with a heater indoors. If needed, remote learning will be used by schools.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20220504030215/https://education.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/advice-for-families

H8_Notes: (Note: Information regarding aged care restrictions during 3 June - 9 June could not be found, so most recent information from 14 May is given instead.)    By NSW government restrictions, residents of aged care facilities were only allowed two fully vaccinated visitors aged 12 or over (must have received second dose at least 14 days prior to visit) plus two children under 12 each day. This means that non-vaccinated individuals are not allowed to visit aged care facilities. Visitors are strongly encouraged to have taken the booster shot, receive the 2022 flu vaccine and have a negative RAT result prior to each visit. While indoors, all visitors must wear a facial mask apart from particular circumstances but the visit should take outdoors whenever possible. People providing a service to a resident are not considered visitors. Exemptions can be made to the two-visitor rule if the resident is at end of life, subject to condition that operator of facility takes reasonable steps to ensure that no more than 4 people are allowed to visit at any one time, all visitors are wearing masks and there is minimal interaction between visitors, staff and other residents. Visitors are not allowed entry into an aged care facility if they have COVID-19 symptoms, are a household or close contact, have been overseas in the past 14 days, waiting for COVID-19 test result or have otherwise been exposed to COVID-19 in 7 days prior to visit.    Residents, provided they do not show COVID-19 symptoms and are provided with appropriate personal protective equipment, are allowed to leave the facility but must abide by government guidelines. They are also recommended to get booster shot as soon as possible.    Staff are recommended to take RAT before start of each shift and are required to be fully vaccinated and taken booster shot as well as wear mask inside facility. The national government agreed that visits in aged care facilities should be limited to a short duration, a maximum of two visitors at one time per day, and conducted in line with social distancing practices. V1_Notes: There are five phases in the Australian vaccine rollout plan that focus on protecting the most vulnerable Australians.   phase 1a:  - Quarantine & border workers  - Frontline health care workers sub-groups for prioritisation  - Aged care & disability care staff  - Aged care & disability resident   Phase 1b:  - Elderly adults aged 80 years & over   - Elderly adults aged 70-79 years  - Other healthcare workers  - Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander people >55  - Younger adults with an underlying medical condition, including those with a disability  - Critical and high-risk worker inc police, defence, fire, emergency serv & meat processing  Phase 2a:  - Adults aged 60-69 years   - Adults aged 50-59 years   - Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander 18-54  - Other critical & high-risk workers  Phase 2b:  Balance of adults population   Phase 3:  < Children under 18, if recommended.     Ethnic minorities in Australia are represented by the Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander (ATSI) community. As the AUS vaccine prioritisation plan divide the group eligibility based on two different age groups (above 55+ in phase 1b; and 18-54 group in phase 2a), the 'At Risk xx-xx" age range is used instead of the 'ethnic minoritiesâ€™ to represent ATSI.   Additionally, category substitution used for the following groups:   1. 'Other high contact profession...' for 'disability care staff'  2. 'Factory workers' for 'meat processing' worker    https://web.archive.org/web/20220807033911/https://www.health.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2021/03/priority-groups-for-covid-19-vaccination-program-phase-1b_1.pdf

E1_Notes: People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 1 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments

The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period. E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).    The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.    The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.    A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.    The directions in place between 30 January and 5 February 2022 were a continuation of existing directions. H7_Notes: According to the Australian Government Department of Health website (as last updated 3 February 2022), the Australian Government had been distributing COVID-19 vaccines through Operation COVID Shield, the national taskforce coordinating the Australian vaccine rollout.    As part of the rollout, all Australians* aged 5 years and over could book a free COVID-19 vaccination appointment, although it was slightly more difficult for those in the 5-11 year age group to receive a vaccine compared to other eligible age groups, as not all vaccine providers were able to provide the smaller Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose for 5-11 year olds.    The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.    As 93.65% of Australians aged 16 years and above had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, 77.11% of Australians aged 12-15 years old had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, and 44.15% of Australians aged 5-11 years old had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, the Australian Government was likely able to deliver on its universal vaccination policy. The Essential Visitors List sets out the minimum visitors who are permitted to access care facilities, including during outbreak scenarios, and includes:  end of life support and visits  parents or guardians of the resident if they are aged under 18 years  parent, guardian (including guardians appointed by VCAT), partner, carer, support or other named person of a resident who is aged 18 or over to provide emotional and social support  a person providing care and/or support for a residentâ€™s physical, cognitive, social or emotional wellbeing (including mental health support and support for people living with dementia)  nominated person in the case of a residentâ€™s mental illness or incapacity  persons providing learning and/or training to support the residentâ€™s care and/or discharge  interpreters or informal language support  contractors whose work requires on-site attendance  aged and disability care advocates  legal representatives of residents and persons with power of attorney for residents  volunteers in the Community Visitors Scheme.  You may be exempt from entry requirements if you are:  - a person visiting for the purpose of end-of-life visit  - an essential carer of a resident, or a person nominated by the director of the care facility where undertaking a rapid antigen test is not practicable  - providing professional patient care as an emergency worker, healthcare professional, or an ambulance worker  - able to provide evidence of a negative result from a PCR test taken within 24 hours before visiting.  Visitors must sign a declaration upon entry to state that they have not been in contact with a confirmed case in the past 7 days.  You must not visit a care facility to see residents if you:  - tested positive for COVID-19  - have COVID-19 symptoms  - have had contact with a confirmed case outside the home and are waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result. H8_Notes: Under the Visitors to Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions #2, in force since 25 April 2020, most non-residents are banned from entering aged care facilities. Exceptions include:  -	people who work at the facility (officers, employees, and contractors)  -	people providing essential goods and services to the facility  -	people providing health care or medicine to a resident  -	people visiting a resident to provide care and support (for up to 2 hours) or end-of-life support (e.g. religious or spiritual services)  -	emergency and law enforcement officials (e.g. police officers, ambulance staff, firefighters)  -	lawyers providing will or estate planning services to residents  -	prospective residents of the facility    Even if they belong to one of the categories allowed to enter, people must not enter aged care facilities if they:  -	have been outside Australia in the past 14 days  -	have been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case in the past 14 days  -	have respiratory symptoms or a fever higher than 38 degrees  -	are not vaccinated against influenza (unless they are emergency/law enforcement officials)  -	are under 16 years old, unless providing end-of-life support to a resident    This is a continuation of policy since 25th April 2020, and applies statewide with no regional variation.  See http://web.archive.org/web/20220913085505/https://www.wa.gov.au/system/files/2020-07/Revoked-Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No2_0.pdf

The notice was removed from the WA Government's Controlled Border webpage on 11 June 2021, when Queensland was classified as a 'very low risk' jurisdiction. This meant that individuals travelling to WA from Queensland were required to complete a G2G pass registration and declaration prior to leaving (which would later be scanned in WA), wear a mask when in WA airspace or entering WA airports, as well as undergo health screening upon arrival in WA. Victoria continued to be classified as a 'medium-risk' jurisdiction, where travellers from Victoria were prohibited from entering WA unless they had an exemption approved through the G2G pass system. According to the WA Government's website as of 11 June 2021, Victoria transitioned from a 'medium risk' to a 'low risk' state at 6:00pm on 11 June 2021.  This meant that travellers entering WA from Victoria had to complete a G2G pass which stipulated that they did not have COVID-19 and declared the locations they have been to in the past 14 days. After arrival, travellers from Victoria were required to complete a health screening, then quarantine for 14 days. They also had to present for COVID-19 testing 11 days after arrival if they were still in WA.    All other jurisdictions were classified as 'very low risk', meaning that travellers from Australian jurisdictions other than Victoria were required to complete a mandatory G2G pass and declaration before travelling, then complete a health screening on arrival. These travellers were not required to quarantine.     This represents a relaxation of  COVID-19 -related border policy from directions which were initially introduced on 27 May 2021 and 9 June 2021, where travel from Victoria was prohibited and travellers from Queensland were required to quarantine for 14 days after arrival. E1_Notes: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. There is also a COVID-19 Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for workers unable to earn an income due to state or territory public health orders (e.g. a lockdown). The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week. The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn.     http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours    http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments    https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. H7_Notes: According to the Australian Government Department of Health website (as last updated 3 February 2022), the Australian Government had been distributing COVID-19 vaccines through Operation COVID Shield, the national taskforce coordinating the Australian vaccine rollout.    As part of the rollout, all Australians* aged 5 years and over could book a free COVID-19 vaccination appointment, although it was slightly more difficult for those in the 5-11 year age group to receive a vaccine compared to other eligible age groups, as not all vaccine providers were able to provide the smaller Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose for 5-11 year olds.    The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.    As 93.65% of Australians aged 16 years and above had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, 77.11% of Australians aged 12-15 years old had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, and 44.15% of Australians aged 5-11 years old had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, the Australian Government was likely able to deliver on its universal vaccination policy. H2_Notes: According to Interim infection prevention and control guidelines for the management of COVID-19 in healthcare settings published by Queensland Health (Version 1.8; 19 February 2020), it states that patients who meet the suspected case definition should have laboratory testing performed.  The meaning of suspect is referred to Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National guidelines for public health units. It also suggests that patients meeting the suspect case definition should be tested for SARS-CoV-2.    According to the definition (see note), it appears that only people who meet certain criteria can get tested, such as showing COVID-19 symptoms, being a close contact, etc.    Additionally, according to Coronavirus (COVID-19) update for GPs published by the Queensland Government on 17 March 2020, it states that GPs can request a COVID-19 test at no out-of-pocket cost to the patient if the requesting medical practitioner suspects their patient is at risk of having COVID-19.     This represents a level 2 restriction in Queensland.    Note:  The definition of â€˜suspect caseâ€™:  A. If the patient satisfies epidemiological and clinical criteria, they are classified as a suspect case.    Epidemiological criteria  -	International travel in the 14 days before illness onset.  OR  -	Close contact (see Contact definition below) in 14 days before illness onset with a confirmed case of COVID-19.    Clinical criteria  -	Fever.  OR  -	Acute respiratory infection (e.g. shortness of breath, cough, sore throat) with or  without fever.    B. If the patient has severe bilateral community-acquired pneumonia (critically ill*) and no other cause is identified, with or without recent international travel, they are classified as a suspect case.    *requiring care in ICU/HDU, or for patients in which ICU care is not appropriate, respiratory or multiorgan failure. Clinical judgement should be exercised considering the likelihood of COVID-19.    C. If any healthcare worker with direct patient contact has a fever (=37.5) AND an acute respiratory infection (e.g. shortness of breath, cough, sore throat), they are classified as a suspect case (see Healthcare workers for further information). H8_Notes: As of 21 March 2020, the Aged Care Direction becomes effective. The Direction is to restrict contact between residents and non-residents of a residential aged care facility and direct measures that aged care facilities must put in place for visitors to the facility.    The Direction prohibits people from entering or remaining on the premises of a residential aged care facility in Queensland. Certain groups of people are exempted from the prohibition, such as employees or contractors in the facilities, people visiting the residential aged care facility for the purposes of end of life support for a resident of the facility, people visiting the residential aged care facility to provide goods or services, etc. Those exempted groups are also subject to other requirements such as having a temperature equal to or higher than 37.5 degrees or symptoms of acute respiratory infection, being under 16 years (unless the visit is for the purposes of end of life support for a resident), etc.    It also states that the operator of a residential aged care facility in Queensland must not permit a resident, excluding an end of life resident, to leave the facility except to receive or access health care or in the case of emergency.     Since the Direction largely prohibits external visitors from entering or remaining on the premises of a residential aged care facility in Queensland, and more importantly, it restricts the residentsâ€™ movement with minimal exceptions, it is more likely to be considered as a level 3G of restriction.    This represents a stringent policy of significant changes to pre-covid times as of 21 March 2020 in Queensland. C2_Notes: "As at 8 November 2020, there are measures in place relating to businesses:  - social distancing must be in place allowing only 1 person per 4 square meters indoors, 1 person per 2 square metres outdoors, at most 50 people if indoor floor space is less than 200 square metres  - encouraging social distancing with visual markers  - increased hygiene procedures  e.g. cleaning surfaces and providing hand sanitisers  - keep a customer contact register and store information for 56 days then dispose securely  - require flu jab for some staff where relevant  - COVID safe industry plans are required for businesses wanting to offer their services to more than 50 people at a time  - all businesses must have a COVID safe management plan and a COVID safe checklists  - For restricted businesses not wanting to serve more than 50 people, they must have COVID safe checklists. E1_Notes: People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 1 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments

C7_Notes: The Border Restrictions Direction (No.58), which was effective between 13 December 2021 and 30 December 2021, stated that individuals who had been to a listed COVID-19 hotspot (NSW, ACT, VIC, Greater Adelaide, and parts of NT) in the past 14 days could not travel to Queensland unless they met the following criteria:     - They had been fully vaccinated  - They had received a negative COVID-19 test from the COVID-19 hotspot within 72 hours of arriving in Queensland  - If remaining in Queensland on the fifth day after arrival, they were required to get tested for COVID-19 as close to the fifth day after arrival as possible.  - They were not an international arrival    Unvaccinated border zone residents (from NSW LGAs on the border with Queensland) who had been to a restricted border zone LGA (Moree Plains Shire, except for Tulloona, Garah, Boomi, Mungindi, Toomelah and Boggabilla) without entering any other COVID-19 hotspots in the past 14 days were only allowed to travel to Queensland for essential purposes. They were only allowed to stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to fulfill the essential purposes. These residents were required to follow home quarantine directions if staying overnight or longer.    Fully vaccinated border zone residents who had been to a restricted border zone LGA without entering any other COVID-19 hotspots in the past 14 days were only allowed to travel to Queensland for limited purposes. They were only allowed to stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to fulfill the limited purposes.    Unvaccinated border zone residents who had not been to a restricted LGA or a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days could only enter to for a permitted purpose, and could only stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to complete the permitted purpose.    Fully vaccinated border zone residents who had not been to a restricted LGA or a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days could enter Queensland with no further restrictions.    Individuals who had been to an interstate exposure location, or were identified as close, casual, or secondary contacts of a COVID-19 case, and had to fulfill isolation requirements in another Australian State or Territory were not permitted to enter Queensland, regardless of whether or not they had fulfilled any other requirements necessary to enter Queensland.    This was a continuation of existing COVID-19 restrictions. Another Queensland Government webpage (as of 29 December 2021) stated that authorities would contact positive COVID-19 cases to identify contacts, although it is unclear whether this was being done for every single case.  Although businesses and activities were required to collect contact information from staff and visitors for contact tracing during this period of time, some local news reports suggested that this was not always feasible, and that extensive contact tracing was not always conducted. According to a news article published in the Brisbane Times on 22 December 2021, the Chief Health Officer of Queensland reportedly stated that "as the [COVID-19 case] numbers increase, the amount of investigation that the public health units will do will reduce" in regards to local contact tracing.    Considering that Queensland recorded 189 new cases on 22 December 2021, and this number increased steadily to 1,158 new cases on 28 December 2021, it is likely that the Queensland Government was unable to conduct comprehensive contact tracing for every single positive COVID-19 case during this time period.    Official Queensland Government statements (published on Government websites between 22-28 December 2021) regarding the comprehensiveness of contact tracing were a continuation of existing messaging. However, since the daily COVID-19 case numbers were much higher during this time period than they were in the month prior (with 6 new cases recorded on 6 December 2021, and 0 new cases recorded on 22 November 2021), it is likely that contact tracing became less comprehensive at some point during, or directly prior to 22-28 December. Under the new definition, a diagnosed person is someone who has tested positive to COVID-19, either through a PCR or a rapid antigen test (RAT).    You are a close contact if you are a household member or a household-like contact of a diagnosed person:  -	A household member is a person who ordinarily resides at the same premises or place of accommodation as the diagnosed person, and who are residing at the premises or place of accommodation at the time the diagnosed person receives their positive COVID-19 test result. You do not have to be related to the diagnosed person to be considered a household member.  -	A household-like contact is a person who has spent more than four hours with the diagnosed person in a house or other place of accommodation, care facility or similar.  Note: a person is not a household-like contact if they are in a separate part of the house, accommodation or care facility that has a separate point of entry and no shared common areas, and if they do not have contact or interaction for more than four hours.    This means that unless your workers are living in the same household as a confirmed covid case, they will not be considered close contacts and will not have to get tested (unless they have symptoms). The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. C1_Notes: Students are expected to be learning on school sites.    Same day student absence notification ( departmental employees only) requirements apply. Schools must notify parents or carers of an unexplained absence of their child as soon as practicable on the day of absence.    While students are learning onsite, schools are not required to provide home-based learning options unless there are specific circumstances justifying the student's absence.    Students unable to attend school because they are a close contact of a positive case of COVID-19 and following Queensland Health quarantine requirements  are not expected to do schoolwork while in quarantine. However, schools may choose to provide access to learning resources (such as learning@home ) to help students to continue their learning.    Students unable to attend school or participate in the learning program due to medical reasons should be supported by their school, just as they would be in the case of any extended medical absence. The school's approach to learning for the student should consider the expected duration of absence, the student's learning needs, available tools and resources, and the school's established approach to supporting continuity of learning.    At all times, including where a student is learning@home, any concerns of risk of harm to the student must be addressed in line with the department's student protection procedures. All student protection measures and training for staff and visitors must be maintained at all times.    Students of all ages are able to attend school regardless of their vaccination status. Any student over 16 years of age is not required to be vaccinated in order to attend school. Schools and students need to follow the heath directions for work placements and/or traineeships.    If a parent or carer chooses to keep their child at home due to their concerns about COVID-19, where necessary, schools will engage with the parent or carer and offer support to ensure their child returns to school as soon as possible.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220404114617/https://qed.qld.gov.au/covid19/school-operations/covid-normal

H3_Notes: You are a close contact if you have been with a person that has COVID-19 or you've spent more than 4 hours with a person who has COVID-19 in a house or other accommodation (such as an apartment, shared accommodation, residential aged care facility or hospital). H8_Notes: This is a continuation of the existing policy commenced in April. The national government agreed that visits in aged care facilities should be limited to a short duration, a maximum of two visitors at one time per day, and conducted in line with social distancing practices. Infection prevention and control measures must be balanced against the needs and best interests of residents. Aged care providers are best placed to make these assessments on a case by case basis. The following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter the aged care facilities: â€¢ Those who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days; â€¢ Those who have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days; â€¢ Those with fever or any (even mild) symptoms of acute respiratory infection (e.g. cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath); and â€¢ Those who have not been vaccinated against influenza (after 1 May). The national government stressed that it is not acceptable for any facility to put in place restrictions beyond the principles agreed. These include complete lockdowns or banning all visits from carers and families, other than during a specified facility outbreak. Facilities need to know the appropriate levels of infection control and prevention to implement, in consultation with the relevant public health units and the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission. The Commonwealth Government will continue to monitor the situation and will take steps, if necessary, to require facilities to seek an exemption from the Commission before implementing additional restrictions. Additionally, on 1 May, the Morrison government announces the additional covid-19 specific support packaging totalling $205 million under targeted measures. The support is aimed at ensuring aged care providers can offer reinforced levels of safety and care for those who need it most. H8_Notes: On 10 June (published 19 June), the Australian Health Protection Principal Committee (AHPPC) updated their advice for residential aged care facilities.  AHPPC recommends that Residential Aged Care facilities (RACFs) implement measures to reduce the risk of transmission to residents, including:  â€¢	limiting visits to a maximum of two visitors at any one time per resident  â€¢	visits should be conducted in a residentâ€™s room, outdoors, or a specified area in the RACF, rather than communal areas with other residents  â€¢	no large group visits should be permitted at this time, however gatherings of residents in communal or outdoor areas which adhere to social distancing and current jurisdictional requirements for gathering size may be permitted  AHPPC maintains that the following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter a RACF:  â€¢	Individuals who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days.  â€¢	Individuals who have been in close contact with a confirmed case within the last 14 days.  â€¢	Individuals who are unwell, particularly those with fever or acute respiratory infection (for example, cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath) symptoms.  â€¢	Individuals who have not been vaccinated against influenza.  AHPPC recommends that:   â€¢	children of all ages be permitted to enter RACFs  â€¢	visiting service providers be permitted to enter RACFs when their services cannot be provided via telehealth or other adaptive models of care, and the resident cannot attend an external facility to receive these services  â€¢	spouses or other close relatives or social supports are not limited in the number of hours that they spend with their spouse/relative  AHPPC recommends that facilities return to a higher level of protection (such as restricting visiting service providers) if there are recent cases of COVID-19 acquired in the local vicinity of the facility.    https://web.archive.org/web/20201201141832/https://www.health.gov.au/news/health-alerts/novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov-health-alert/how-to-protect-yourself-and-others-from-coronavirus-covid-19/limits-on-public-gatherings-for-coronavirus-covid-19  https://web.archive.org/web/20200908041158/https://www.health.gov.au/news/australian-health-protection-principal-committee-ahppc-update-to-residential-aged-care-facilities-about-minimising-the-impact-of-covid-19  https://web.archive.org/web/20201103111726/https://www.health.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2020/06/coronavirus-covid-19-information-for-families-and-residents-on-restricted-visits-to-residential-aged-care-facilities.pdf

C7_Notes: During this time period, all non-essential travellers travelling to Tasmania will be forced to enter quarantine for 14 days, provided they have evidence of residency, do not have COVID-19 and have not been overseas or on a cruise ship with 14 days of arriving. Tasmanian residents not coming back from Victoria are allowed to quarantine at their residences. Essential travellers are able to avoid the 14 day quarantine but still must report any possible COVID-19 symptoms that appear.    The large exception is for anybody who has travelled to Victoria in the past 14 days before arrival, who are not allowed into Tasmania while Tasmanian residents who come back from Victoria must quarantine in government provided accomodation. Where only cash tickets are available, passengers are asked to purchase 10-ride tickets to reduce the number of transactions.   Additionally, as stated on Tas covid-19 website, Metro Tasmania continues to implement an enhanced cleaning regime of its bus fleet by its contractor. C7_Notes: This is a continuation of the existing policy with no regional variation.  Border restrictions are in place in Tasmania based on the locations travellers have spent time in during the 14 days prior to their arrival in Tasmania.  All non-essential travellers, including returning Tasmanians, must have prior approval to enter the State. If granted, non-Essentials travellers need to go through 14 day quarantine in government-designated accommodation at their own expense. Essential Travellers who are approved to enter the State after spending time in a high-risk location are required to undertake a clinical assessment, including COVID-19 test on arrival.
