H8_Notes: During this time period, various restrictions were placed by the Tasmanian government to protect aged care residential facilities (RACFs). No more than two people (including children under 16 years and visiting services) could visit a resident at a time (although multiple visits were allowed). All individuals are screened before entering the facility to check for COVID-19 symptoms, such as a fever or sore throat where they will not be allowed to enter, and must have taken the 2020 influenza vaccination before either visiting or work at a RACF. Visitors must also not be in quarantine, meaning that they also cannot have been interstate or overseas or have been in close contact with case in past 14 days. Maximum duration of visit is subject to RACF policy.    Exemptions can be granted by the Director of Public Health if the individual is well, a significant person to a resident and seeks to provide end of life support to that resident. People arriving from interstate must also present a G2G pass.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20201012040127/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/aged-care-facility-visits

C1_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Department of Education website between 25 February and 14 March 2021, schoolchildren were not required to maintain social distancing, and were encouraged to adopt good hygiene practices. However, all adults working in schools were required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m, and school events were required to follow venue density requirements (one person per two square metres with a capacity limit of 250 individuals). School events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for drinking and dancing.     Schools received extra cleaning of high-touch areas and toilets, as well as access to supplies such as soap, hand sanitiser, and disinfectant wipes.    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled, as were large sports and arts events with long lead time organisational arrangements.    The measures in place between 1 and 14 March 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210225214308/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/  https://web.archive.org/web/20210308043921/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/  https://web.archive.org/web/20210314165425/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/
C2_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 2 March 2021, businesses and workplaces were permitted to operate as long as they adhered to minimum COVID-19 safety standards and recorded these in a COVID Safety Plan. Under these minimum standards, businesses were required to collect contact information from staff and patrons in order to assist with contact tracing efforts, ensure that physical distancing requirements were being met, ensure that workers who were required to quarantine or self-isolate did not enter the workplace, maintain a cleaning schedule, and manage the entry of individuals who were suspected of having COVID-19 or had COVID-19 symptoms.    A density rule of one person per two square metres applied to many venues, and there were capacity restrictions on events with more than 250 people attending. Masks were also required to be worn in airports, and at large indoor events with more than one person per two square metres.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions    Archived links:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210302154646/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/business-restrictions  http://web.archive.org/web/20210303131915/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/covid-19-safe-workplaces-framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20210302173547/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20210303133118/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing  https://web.archive.org/web/20210312132133/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/facemasks

C1_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Department of Education website between 14 March and 11 April 2021, schoolchildren were not required to maintain social distancing, and were encouraged to adopt good hygiene practices. However, all adults working in schools were required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m, and school events were required to follow venue density requirements (one person per two square metres with a capacity limit of 250 individuals). School events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for drinking and dancing.     Schools received extra cleaning of high-touch areas and toilets, as well as access to supplies such as soap, hand sanitiser, and disinfectant wipes.    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled, as were large sports and arts events with long lead time organisational arrangements.    The measures in place between 15 and 28 March 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210314165549/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/  https://web.archive.org/web/20210411030917/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/
C2_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 17 March 2021, businesses and workplaces were permitted to operate as long as they adhered to minimum COVID-19 safety standards and recorded these in a COVID Safety Plan. A density rule of one person per two square metres applied to many venues, and there were capacity restrictions on events with more than 250 people attending. Masks were also required to be worn in airports, and at large indoor events with more than one person per two square metres.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions. C1_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Department of Education website between 14 March and 11 April 2021, schoolchildren were not required to maintain social distancing, and were instead encouraged to adopt good hygiene practices. However, all adults working in schools were required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m, and school events were required to follow venue density requirements (one person per two square metres with a capacity limit of 250 individuals). School events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for drinking and dancing.     Schools received extra cleaning of high-touch areas and toilets, as well as access to supplies such as soap, hand sanitiser, and disinfectant wipes.    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled, as were large sports and arts events with long lead time organisational arrangements.    The measures in place between 29 March and 11 April 2021 were a continuation of existing directions. C2_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 30 March 2021, businesses and workplaces were permitted to operate as long as they adhered to minimum COVID-19 safety standards and recorded these in a COVID Safety Plan. Under these minimum standards, businesses were required to collect contact information from staff and patrons in order to assist with contact tracing efforts, ensure that physical distancing requirements were being met, ensure that workers who were required to quarantine or self-isolate did not enter the workplace, maintain a cleaning schedule, and manage the entry of individuals who were suspected of having COVID-19 or had COVID-19 symptoms.    A density rule of one person per two square metres applied to many venues, and there were capacity restrictions on events with more than 250 people attending. Masks were also required to be worn in airports, and at large indoor events with more than one person per two square metres.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions. H3_Notes: According to a COVID-19 update published by the Tasmanian Government, Tasmania changed their definition of a close contact to match a nationally consistent definition of an individual who has "spent four hours or longer with a COVID-19 case in a household or household-like setting". This new definition came into effect on 1 January 2022, in light of a National Cabinet meeting which attempted to create a more unified set of guidelines for dealing with close contacts.    Individuals with COVID-19 were required to inform their close, social, and work/education contacts that they had been infected. Individuals with COVID-19 were to instruct their close contacts to self-isolate for 7 days, take a RAT on days 1 and 6 of isolation, and take a PCR test if symptomatic.    Those with COVID-19 were required to tell their social contacts to get a PCR test and self-isolate until receiving a negative result if symptomatic. A social contact was defined as an individual who the COVID-19 case had "15 minutes of face-to-face contact with, or spent 2 hours with, in the same indoor space".    Workplaces and educational institutions with COVID-19 cases were required to tell employees and students to get a PCR test and self-isolate until receiving a negative result if symptomatic.    These measures likely represented a relaxation of contact tracing efforts, as the narrower close contact definition, and the increased responsibility of COVID-19 cases to inform their contacts of the appropriate testing and isolation requirements, meant that public health officials spent less time communicating with COVID-19 cases and their contacts. C3_Notes: There was no mention of a ban on public events on the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 20 January 2022). However, the Tasmanian Government developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6. In general, every individual at an event or gathering was required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from other patrons or staff where possible, and events were required to follow a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.     Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted, included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and events with more than 1000 people attending.     Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.     Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health   The directions in place between 6 to 13 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. C7_Notes: According to a media release published by the Tasmanian Director of Public Health on 12 January 2022, the Public Health Service no longer recommended limiting travel to King Island. Travellers who did not have evidence of a negative COVID-19 test taken within the required time periods were required to quarantine until receiving a negative test result. C2_Notes: According to a media update published by the Tasmanian Government on 13 January 2022, the Tasmania was creating a temporary exemption framework for close contacts working in critical industries. This framework enabled critical employees in essential business undergoing critical workforce shortages to apply for an exemption from isolation or quarantine requirements if they became close contacts of a COVID-19 case. The framework was available for businesses in the following sectors:   - Day procedures centres included in the Health Services Establishments Act   - Emergency services   - Power, utilities, and essential infrastructure services   - Agriculture and fisheries   - Freight and logistics involved in delivering essential goods   - Major manufacturing, distribution, and critical supply chains related to essential goods   - Correctional and detention facilities   - Essential commercial cleaning services   - Public transport services.     Before registering for the framework, businesses were required to assess the risks of a critical workforce shortage, seek possible alternatives to requesting close contacts to fill the shortage, and implement extra COVID-Safe measures such as increased testing of workers.     This update was a relaxation of existing COVID-19 policy directions. All other workplace restrictions pertaining to COVID-19 remained the same:     According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022) all businesses were permitted to operate, but were required to adopt measures to meet minimum COVID-19 safety standards as stated in the Direction under Section 16 - COVID-19 Workplace Plans - No.2, and record these in a safety plan. As part of these minimum safety standards, businesses were required to practice 1.5m social distancing or impose a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres (although exempted workplaces were only required to ensure that the number of individuals in the workplace did not exceed the number specified on their occupancy permits), maintain cleaning and hygiene practices workplace to minimise the spread of COVID-19, train and inform staff and patrons of COVID-safe requirements they must follow in order to minimise transmission, prevent individuals who had COVID-19 symptoms or were known to be under isolation requirements from entering the premises, and collect contact information from individuals entering or leaving the workplace in order to assist with contact tracing efforts.     Masks were also required in indoor spaces. Individuals entering pubs, nightclubs, bars, and some licensed events were required to be fully vaccinated. Other industry-specific COVID-safe guidelines, such as regular COVID-19 testing for those working in quarantine facilities, and the adoption of transmission-based precautions  in healthcare settings were also in place. C3_Notes: There was no mention of a ban on public events on the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 20 January 2022). However, the Tasmanian Government developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6. In general, every individual at an event or gathering was required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from other patrons or staff where possible, and events were required to follow a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.     Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted, included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and events with more than 1000 people attending.     Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.     Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.   The directions in place between 14 and 21 January were a continuation of existing restrictions. C2_Notes: The Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 28 January 2022) stated that business were allowed to operate, but were required to implement measures to meet minimum COVID-19 safety standards and record them in a safety plan. According to the Direction Under Section 16 - Workplace COVID Plan - No.2, these minimum standards included the following:    	- Maintaining a physical distance of 1.5m where possible, or a density limit of 1 person per 2 square limits (unless the workplace was exempt from doing so)  	- Reviewing public health advice regularly in order to find ways to keep the business COVID-safe, as well as training workers to minimise the risk of COVID-19 transmission in the workplace, and informing patrons of COVID-related safety measures and restrictions  	- Cleaning and disinfecting the workplace as necessary to reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission  	- Preventing individuals with COVID-19 symptoms, or those who are required to quarantine or self-isolate, from entering the business  	- Collecting contact information from individuals entering the workplace for contact tracing purposes (unless exempt from doing so)    Businesses were encouraged to review and update their Workplace COVID Plans as of 20 January 2022.    Masks were required in all indoor spaces and outdoor events attended by more than 1000 patrons, except where an individual had to perform a job that required clear enunciation or mouth visibility.    Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Unvaccinated individuals were also prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities unless they had tested negative for COVID-19 (see H8 for more details). Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate,   Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health. Individuals working in early childhood education setting were required to have received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine from 8 January 2022. C3_Notes: There was no mention of a ban on public events on the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 28 January 2022).    However, the Tasmanian Government developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6.    In general, every individual at an event or gathering was required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from other patrons or staff where possible, and events were required to follow a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.    Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted,  included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required  to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and events with more than 1000 people attending.    Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.    Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.    The directions in place between 22 and 28 January were a continuation of existing restrictions. E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. Tasmanians were instead asked to utilise existing concession or financial assistance support, seek help from community organisations, or check their local councils if they required debt or contract relief. H3_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Government website between 24 and 29 January 2022, individuals with COVID-19 were told to 'help with contact tracing', and were responsible for informing close contacts,  social contacts, as well as their places of employment and education that they were infected.   Businesses and workplaces were not listed as exposure sites, and were instead responsible for informing workplace contacts about positive cases, as well as implementing the necessary COVID-safe measures to keep employees safe. They were expected to assist with the contact tracing process by collecting staff or visitor information not provided by the Check In Tas app. However, Public Health would only contact a business if they knew of several cases linked to the business in question.    On 28 January 2022, the Tasmanian Government website was updated to remove a statement which explained that a 'close contact' could include an individual who spent more than 4 hours at the same site, workplace, or venue as a COVID-19 case during a significant transmission event. The new version of the website only stated that a 'close contact' was someone who spent more than 4 hours in a residential setting with a COVID-19 case during their infectious period.    The contact tracing in place between 22 and 29 January 2022 was a continuation of existing measures, although the change in the definition of a close contact represented a relaxation of existing measures, and an indirect reduction of government involvement with potential contacts of COVID-19 cases. H8_Notes: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 29 January 2022, visitors were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had contact with a confirmed or suspected COVID-19 case within 7 days before entry. In addition to this, visitors could only enter residential aged care facilities if they wore a mask, had no COVID-19 symptoms, were not required to quarantine or isolate, had not visited an exposure site in the past 14 days and were not required to avoid high-risk settings, and had checked into the facility. C2_Notes: According to an update published by the Tasmanian Government  on 25 January 2022, additional industries which were considered 'essential for the supply of critical goods and services to the community', such as health, welfare, care, and support industries, as well as education and childcare services, telecommunications, data, broadcasting, and media services, were able to register for a temporary exemption framework for close contacts from 28 January 2022. Critical staff working in these industries who were close contacts of a COVID-19 case were not required to quarantine if their business was undergoing a critical workforce shortage and had successfully registered for the framework.    Before registering for the framework, businesses were required to conduct a risk assessment to identify the risks of a critical workforce shortage, seek possible alternatives to requesting close contacts to fill the shortage, understand the minimum number of workers needed to provide their services, ensure that the return of the close contact is necessary and justified, implement extra measures to prevent the transmission of COVID-19 whilst the close contact is required to work, and establish a process to ensure the employer is aware once the critical shortage has passed and close contacts can resume quarantine or isolation.    Critical workers could only be granted an exemption if they were fully vaccinated, did not have COVID-19 symptoms, had their attendance registered through Worksafe Tasmania, and returned a negative COVID-19 test result each day before work.    This update was a relaxation of existing COVID-19 policy directions. All other workplace restrictions pertaining to COVID-19 remained the same:    The Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 28 January 2022) stated that business were allowed to operate, but were required to implement measures to meet minimum COVID-19 safety standards and record them in a safety plan. According to the Direction Under Section 16 - Workplace COVID Plan - No.2, these minimum standards included the following:    	- Maintaining a physical distance of 1.5m where possible, or a density limit of 1 person per 2 square limits (unless the workplace was exempt from doing so)  	- Reviewing public health advice regularly in order to find ways to keep the business COVID-safe, as well as training workers to minimise the risk of COVID-19 transmission in the workplace, and informing patrons of COVID-related safety measures and restrictions  	- Cleaning and disinfecting the workplace as necessary to reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission  	- Preventing individuals with COVID-19 symptoms, or those who are required to quarantine or self-isolate, from entering the business  	- Collecting contact information from individuals entering the workplace for contact tracing purposes (unless exempt from doing so)    Businesses were encouraged to review and update their Workplace COVID Plans as of 20 January 2022.    Masks were required in all indoor spaces and outdoor events attended by more than 1000 patrons, except where an individual had to perform a job that required clear enunciation or mouth visibility.    Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Unvaccinated individuals were also prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities unless they had tested negative for COVID-19 (see H8 for more details). Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate,   Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.      Note: Workers were required to be vaccinated at some businesses including quarantine facilities, health care settings, aged care and disability settings, and at licensed settings (such as pubs, clubs, bars, and nightclubs). Individuals working in early childhood education setting were required to have received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine from 8 January 2022. This information was not recorded in C2 or V4 as of 5 February 2022. E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).    The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.    The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.    A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.    The directions in place between 30 January and 5 February 2022 were a continuation of existing directions. H7_Notes: According to the Australian Government Department of Health website (as last updated 3 February 2022), the Australian Government had been distributing COVID-19 vaccines through Operation COVID Shield, the national taskforce coordinating the Australian vaccine rollout.    As part of the rollout, all Australians* aged 5 years and over could book a free COVID-19 vaccination appointment, although it was slightly more difficult for those in the 5-11 year age group to receive a vaccine compared to other eligible age groups, as not all vaccine providers were able to provide the smaller Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose for 5-11 year olds.    The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.    As 93.65% of Australians aged 16 years and above had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, 77.11% of Australians aged 12-15 years old had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, and 44.15% of Australians aged 5-11 years old had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, the Australian Government was likely able to deliver on its universal vaccination policy. Nonetheless, State and Territory Governments also delivered their own updates and specialised services to meet the needs of their jurisdictions. H8_Notes: As of 1 April 2022, as per the Residential Aged Care Facilities â€“ No. 19 commencing on 21 January 2022, there are some restrictions on visits to residential aged care facilities permitted for people providing care and support, with the following restrictions:    - All persons visiting a residential aged care facility, must wear a face mask while they remain on the premises.  - All visitors to a residential aged care facility must provide evidence that they are up to date with their vaccination for COVID-19 and there are no exemptions for a vaccine medical contraindication.  - Visitors must not have any symptoms of COVID-19.    There are non-extensive restrictions in place that aged care facilities are open to unvaccinated visitors who can provide evidence of a negative result from a PCR COVID-19 test taken within the 72 hours prior to the visit or had a negative Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) result within 24 hours prior to visit.    For vaccinated visitors, face masks, social distancing, and the duration of visits rules are in place and some restrictions are subject to each facilitiesâ€™ policies.    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220313024934/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/aged-care-facility-visits    Additionally, there are additional vaccination requirements for workers in residential aged care facilities. As of 1 April 2022, as per paragraph (a) of the Additional Vaccination Requirements for Workers in Certain Settings â€“ No. 1 commencing on 1 April 2022, a person is not permitted to enter, or remain on, the premises of a residential aged care facility unless the person is vaccinated against COVID-19 (â€œthe diseaseâ€) as specified in paragraph (d) if the person â€“  (i) is employed, or engaged, by or on behalf of the residential aged care facility, regardless of whether consideration is paid or payable for the employment or engagement; or  (ii) is undertaking a clinical placement, or work experience, at the residential aged care facility; or  (iii) is employed, or engaged, by or on behalf of the residential aged care facility, to provide services, other than maintenance services, in respect of the residential aged care facility or one or more residents of the residential aged care facility, regardless of whether consideration is paid or payable for the employment or engagement.    Specifically, paragraph (d) provides that a person is vaccinated against the disease if â€“  (i) the person â€“  (A) has received at least one booster dose of a vaccine for the disease; or  (B) is not eligible, in accordance with the ATAGI recommendations, to receive a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease; or  (C) is eligible, in accordance with the ATAGI recommendations, to receive a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease and receives a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease within 4 weeks of becoming eligible; and  (ii) each dose of a vaccine for the disease received by the person has been recorded in â€“  (A) a vaccination certificate issued in respect of the person issued by the Australian Immunisation Register, operated by or on behalf of the Commonwealth Government; or  (B) an equivalent document issued in respect of the person from a jurisdiction outside of Australia that is recognised by the Commonwealth Government or the Director of Public Health; and  (iii) the person provides evidence to his or her relevant supervisor, as required under paragraph (g), of each dose of a vaccine of the disease that the person has received.    As per paragraph (e) of the Additional Vaccination Requirements for Workers in Certain Settings â€“ No. 3, there are several exemptions available for people who are not required to be vaccinated against COVID-19. However, a person who is not required to be vaccinated is required to wear a fitted face covering while he or she is present on the premises of the relevant location for the person (unless this person is a child under 12-year-old) or is not suitable to wear a fitted face covering proved by a medical certificate)     Therefore, the non-vaccinated indicator for H8 should be reported as 2G and the vaccinated indicator for H8 should be reported as 2G. H8_Notes: As of 12 April 2022, as per the Residential Aged Care Facilities â€“ No. 19 commencing on 21 January 2022, there are some restrictions on visits to residential aged care facilities permitted for people providing care and support, with the following restrictions:    - All persons visiting a residential aged care facility, must wear a face mask while they remain on the premises.  - All visitors to a residential aged care facility must provide evidence that they are up to date with their vaccination for COVID-19 and there are no exemptions for a vaccine medical contraindication.  - Visitors must not have any symptoms of COVID-19.    There are non-extensive restrictions in place that aged care facilities are open to unvaccinated visitors who can provide evidence of a negative result from a PCR COVID-19 test taken within the 72 hours prior to visit or had a negative Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) result within 24 hours prior to visit.    For vaccinated visitors, face masks, social distancing, and the duration of visits rules are in place and some restrictions are subject to each facilitiesâ€™ policies.    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220313024934/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/aged-care-facility-visits    Additionally, there are additional vaccination requirements for workers in residential aged care facilities. As of 12 April 2022, as per paragraph (a) of the Additional Vaccination Requirements for Workers in Certain Settings â€“ No. 1 commencing on 1 April 2022, a person is not permitted to enter, or remain on, the premises of a residential aged care facility unless the person is vaccinated against COVID-19 (â€œthe diseaseâ€) as specified in paragraph (d) if the person â€“  (i) is employed, or engaged, by or on behalf of the residential aged care facility, regardless of whether consideration is paid or payable for the employment or engagement; or  (ii) is undertaking a clinical placement, or work experience, at the residential aged care facility; or  (iii) is employed, or engaged, by or on behalf of the residential aged care facility, to provide services, other than maintenance services, in respect of the residential aged care facility or one or more residents of the residential aged care facility, regardless of whether consideration is paid or payable for the employment or engagement.    Specifically, paragraph (d) provides that a person is vaccinated against the disease if â€“  (i) the person â€“  (A) has received at least one booster dose of a vaccine for the disease; or  (B) is not eligible, in accordance with the ATAGI recommendations, to receive a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease; or  (C) is eligible, in accordance with the ATAGI recommendations, to receive a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease and receives a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease within 4 weeks of becoming eligible; and  (ii) each dose of a vaccine for the disease received by the person has been recorded in â€“  (A) a vaccination certificate issued in respect of the person issued by the Australian Immunisation Register, operated by or on behalf of the Commonwealth Government; or  (B) an equivalent document issued in respect of the person from a jurisdiction outside of Australia that is recognised by the Commonwealth Government or the Director of Public Health; and  (iii) the person provides evidence to his or her relevant supervisor, as required under paragraph (g), of each dose of a vaccine of the disease that the person has received. C3_Notes: "As at 28 April 2022, there are requirements in place for events published at 9th March 2022. These apply across Tasmania.  Events with 250 people or less  indoors or 500 people or less outdoors do not have any recommendations or requirements.  Events with seated guests of 5001 to 1000 people require a COVID-19 Safety plan, event registration, approval from the Director of Public Health, and check in Tas QR code implemented.   Events (indoor or outdoor) with 2001 to 5000 people require a safety plan, event registration, approval and check in code  Events with 251-2000 people indoors or 501-2000 people outdoors require a safety checklist, check in code.   The COVID-19 safety plans must be submitted for assessment  at least a minimum of 30 days  prior to the event . The application as part of approval require information about the following :  - Event details including event name, contact details of key event personnel, description, date, event characteristics such as indoor or outdoor, seated or standing, service of alcohol and total number of people  - Completed Event COVID-19 Safety Plan   - Site map showing the size of the event venue in square meters.  This policy represents a continuance of the policy.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220405075952/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework  https://web.archive.org/web/20220505091549/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework"
C4_Notes: "As at 28 April 2022, there are measures in place for gatherings. These are in place across Tasmania.    There is a maximum density limit of not more than 1 person per 2 square metres. However, seated venues are allowed 100% of  a venue's seated capacity.   In any gathering, physical distancing and hygiene is expected. Frequent cleaning is also expected.   Gatherings are limited to 100 people at any one time both indoors or outdoors.   Sporting facilities without seating are limited to the lessor of 1 person per 2 square metres, 250 people in an undivided space indoors or 1000 people in an undivided space outdoors.     Churches are limited to 250 people or 100 percent of seating (whatever is less). This also applies to weddings held in churches.   This represents a continuance of the policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220405083356/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing#Events-(indoor-and-outdoor)"

H8_Notes: As of 5 May 2022, as per the Residential Aged Care Facilities â€“ No. 19 commencing on 21 January 2022, there are some restrictions on visits to residential aged care facilities permitted for people providing care and support, with the following restrictions:    - All persons visiting a residential aged care facility, must wear a face mask while they remain on the premises.  - All visitors to a residential aged care facility must provide evidence that they are up to date with their vaccination for COVID-19 and there are no exemptions for a vaccine medical contraindication.  - Visitors must not have any symptoms of COVID-19.    There are non-extensive restrictions in place that aged care facilities are open to unvaccinated visitors who can provide evidence of a negative result from a PCR COVID-19 test taken within the 72 hours prior to visit or had a negative Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) result within 24 hours prior to visit.    For vaccinated visitors, face masks, social distancing, and the duration of visits rules are in place and some restrictions are subject to each facilitiesâ€™ policies.    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220313024934/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/aged-care-facility-visits    Additionally, there are additional vaccination requirements for workers in residential aged care facilities. As of 5 May 2022, as per paragraph (a) of the Additional Vaccination Requirements for Workers in Certain Settings â€“ No. 1 commencing on 1 April 2022, a person is not permitted to enter, or remain on, the premises of a residential aged care facility unless the person is vaccinated against COVID-19 (â€œthe diseaseâ€) as specified in paragraph (d) if the person â€“  (i) is employed, or engaged, by or on behalf of the residential aged care facility, regardless of whether consideration is paid or payable for the employment or engagement; or  (ii) is undertaking a clinical placement, or work experience, at the residential aged care facility; or  (iii) is employed, or engaged, by or on behalf of the residential aged care facility, to provide services, other than maintenance services, in respect of the residential aged care facility or one or more residents of the residential aged care facility, regardless of whether consideration is paid or payable for the employment or engagement.    Specifically, paragraph (d) provides that a person is vaccinated against the disease if â€“  (i) the person â€“  (A) has received at least one booster dose of a vaccine for the disease; or  (B) is not eligible, in accordance with the ATAGI recommendations, to receive a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease; or  (C) is eligible, in accordance with the ATAGI recommendations, to receive a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease and receives a booster dose of the vaccine for the disease within 4 weeks of becoming eligible; and  (ii) each dose of a vaccine for the disease received by the person has been recorded in â€“  (A) a vaccination certificate issued in respect of the person issued by the Australian Immunisation Register, operated by or on behalf of the Commonwealth Government; or  (B) an equivalent document issued in respect of the person from a jurisdiction outside of Australia that is recognised by the Commonwealth Government or the Director of Public Health; and  (iii) the person provides evidence to his or her relevant supervisor, as required under paragraph (g), of each dose of a vaccine of the disease that the person has received.    As per paragraph (e) of the Additional Vaccination Requirements for Workers in Certain Settings â€“ No. 3, there are several exemptions available for people who are not required to be vaccinated against COVID-19. However, a person who is not required to be vaccinated is required to wear a fitted face covering while he or she is present on the premises of the relevant location for the person (unless this person is a child under 12-year-old) or is not suitable to wear a fitted face covering proved by a medical certificate)     Therefore, the non-vaccinated indicator for H8 should be reported as 2G and the vaccinated indicator for H8 should be reported as 2G. C4_Notes: As of 21 May 2022, limits on the number of people allowed in a space (based on the 1 person per 2 square metres) no longer apply. However, an individual business or premises may choose to place maximum capacity numbers on their premises as part of their COVID-19 safety plan. H2_Notes: On 20th of March 2020, according to the Australia's Department of Health, it was mentioned that doctor will tell you if you should be tested. H8_Notes: On 21 April (the continuation of the existing policy), the National Cabinet reconfirmed the principles announced on 18 March 2020 regarding visits to aged care facilities. In line with these principles, visits should be limited to a short duration, a maximum of two visitors at one time per day, and conducted in line with social distancing practices.   Infection prevention and control measures must be balanced against the needs and best interests of residents. Aged care providers are best placed to make these assessments on a case by case basis.    National Cabinet also reiterated that the following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter the aged care facilities:  â€¢	Those who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days;  â€¢	Those who have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days;  â€¢	Those with fever or any (even mild) symptoms of acute respiratory infection (e.g. cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath); and  â€¢	Those who have not been vaccinated against influenza (after 1 May).    https://web.archive.org/web/20220515000643/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures-210420    Additionally, on 24 April, the National government stressed that the AHPPC advice that it is not acceptable for any facility to put in place restrictions beyond the principles agreed on 17 March 2020. H8_Notes: On 10 June (published 19 June), the Australian Health Protection Principal Committee (AHPPC) updated their advice for residential aged care facilities.  AHPPC recommends that Residential Aged Care facilities (RACFs) implement measures to reduce the risk of transmission to residents, including:  â€¢	limiting visits to a maximum of two visitors at any one time per resident  â€¢	visits should be conducted in a residentâ€™s room, outdoors, or a specified area in the RACF, rather than communal areas with other residents  â€¢	no large group visits should be permitted at this time, however gatherings of residents in communal or outdoor areas which adhere to social distancing and current jurisdictional requirements for gathering size may be permitted  AHPPC maintains that the following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter a RACF:  â€¢	Individuals who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days.  â€¢	Individuals who have been in close contact with a confirmed case within the last 14 days.  â€¢	Individuals who are unwell, particularly those with fever or acute respiratory infection (for example, cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath) symptoms.  â€¢	Individuals who have not been vaccinated against influenza. C2_Notes: As of 22nd July 2022, all businesses must follow density requirements and physical distancing principles. Furthermore, businesses that conduct a defined public activity must have a COVID-Safe Plan and these businesses are required to complete contract tracing records. The density requirement for the Defined public activities is 1 person per 2 square metres with the maximum number of attendees at the place of business determined by its size.     These defined public activities include : onsite purchase and consumption of food or beverages; sports, fitness or recreation activities; indoor public meetings; ceremonies; provision of personal care services; provision of public entertainment; provision of recreation transport; the operation of a nightclub; the operation of a casino or gaming area; auctions and inspections of premises for the purpose of sale or rental of any property; and driver instruction.     A number of locations and activities are excluded from the Direction on public activities. These includes : airpots; public transport; medical or health services, including hospitals; emergency services; disability, aged care or residential facilities; prisons, correctional facilities or training centres; courts or tribunals; Parliament or Government House; council meetings (although members of the public attending must adhere to maximum occupancy and density requirements); food markets, supermarkets, grocery stores, retail stores or shopping centres; workplaces, including offices, factories, laboratories, repair or maintenance premises (workshops), mining or construction sites, waste disposal or processing facilities; land or vessels used in the production or treatment of primary produce; schools, universities, educational institutions and childcare facilities; accommodation facilities such as hotels or motels; where people are transiting through a place (such as Rundle Mall); and any other gathering deemed exempt by the State Coordinator. C7_Notes: The SA Government commenced a number of state border restrictions on 31 January 2021 and these continue on 1 February 2021. Anyone who has been in Western Australia in the previous 14 days was not permitted to enter South Australia. Anyone who arrived in SA from WA on or after 26 January must immediately self-quarantine for 14 days, commencing 31 January. COVID-19 tests are required immediately and again on day 5 and day 12 of quarantine. Anyone who was at the Sheraton Four Points Hotel in Perth on or after 24 January must immediately self-quarantine and complete a survey to notify SA Health that you were at this location.  Anyone travelling to South Australia who have been in the Greater Sydney Region, Central Coast Council or Wollongong City Council in the previous 14 days must: (1) get a COVID-19 test within 24 hours and self-quarantine until you receive a negative test result and (2) get tested again on day 5 and day 12. No requirement to remain in quarantine after receiving a negative COVID-19 result in the first test (unless symptoms are present).  http://web.archive.org/web/20210531132132/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/latest-news/covid-19-update-1-february
E2_Notes: In South Australia, state parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected. C4_Notes: For private gatherings including weddings and funerals, there is a maximum number of 200 people, with 1 person per 2 square metres. If you have 51 to 200 people at a residential premises, you are required to have a COVID-Safe Plan, COVID Marshal and your guests must check-in via the COVID SAfe Check-in. A gathering of up to 1,000 people occurring as part of a defined public activity is a permitted gathering but an approved COVID Management Plan is required for more than 1,000 people. These included support for students unable to attend school on the advice of their medical practitioner, not coming to school when sick, increased physical distancing and personal hygiene recommendations, use of QR COVID-Safe check-ins by all adults entering classrooms or buildings on site (including staff and parents), and additional cleaning of hard surfaces and touch points. Policies were also in place for the temporary closure of a school if they had a Covid-19 case among their staff or students.    This represents a continuation of the existing policy. H7_Notes: Between 1 August 2021 and 29 August 2021, both Oxford AstraZeneca and Pfizer vaccines were being administered. The availability and uptake of each brand for certain age groups depended on whether the sub-national jurisdiction was experiencing an outbreak (See ATAGI statement). Generally, the national vaccine rollout was at phase 2a, meaning that adults aged 40 or above and other persons from certain backgrounds, occupations or with certain medical conditions were able to receive the vaccine.     This is a continuation of phase 2a of the vaccine rollout that begun on 8 June 2021. Note that whilst the national vaccine rollout/ availability was at phase 2a, there were significant diversions of Pfizer vaccines to areas experiencing outbreaks for residents there beyond the phase 2a cohort.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004201858/https://www.health.gov.au/news/covid-19-vaccines-to-be-available-to-everyone-aged-40-years-and-over  https://web.archive.org/web/20211004202146/https://www.health.gov.au/news/atagi-statement-on-use-of-covid-19-vaccines-in-an-outbreak-setting
H8_Notes: Current restrictions in South Australia do not allow visits to aged care facilities:  - If you have a fever or symptoms of a respiratory infection such as a cough, sore throat or shortness of breath  - If you have been directed by an authorised officer to quarantine  - If you been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days or anyone with a high temperature, fever, chills, symptoms of acute respiratory infection, or loss of taste and smell, in the last 72 hours.    All people (excluding residents) at a Residential Aged Care Facility must wear a mask.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210816110930/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/restrictions-and-responsibilities/visits-to-residential-care-facilities

C5_Notes: During this period, there were no transport closures mandated by the South Australian Government. All public transport, including buses and metro systems remained operational.  However, additional measures were implemented to reduce Covid-19 associated risks. These included increased cleaning across all public transport modes with a particular focus on touch points, MetroCard Only system (no cash), mandatory mask wearing, alterations to train and bus layouts to aid in physical distancing, alterations to train schedules to spread out passenger peak periods, and hand sanitisation facilities. The SA Government also encouraged good personal hygiene, practice of physical distancing, and not to travel while sick.  This represents a continuation of the existing policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210707124640/https://adelaidemetro.com.au/Announcements2/Service-updates/COVID-19-public-transport-information  https://web.archive.org/web/20210810143243/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/restrictions-and-responsibilities/activities-and-gatherings/current-activity-restrictions
H6_Notes: In South Australia, masks (covering the mouth and nose) are required in:  - High risk settings  - Personal care services (but not by the customer if it inhibits the service)  - Health care services  - Passenger transport services  - Indoor fitness facilities (except while exercising)  - Shared indoor public places (except for wedding parties) The mention of masks being required for "shared indoor public places" suggests a general indoor mask mandate for public spaces (and hence a code of 3). E1_Notes: Individuals may be eligible for various types of income support. There are three main types. The 'COVID-19 Disaster Payment' is a lump sum payment to help workers unable to earn income due to a COVID-19 state or territory public health order. This may involve a lockdown, hotspot or movement restrictions. The 'Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment' and the 'Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19)' provides income support for those who are required to enter quarantine or isolation.     This is a continuation of the national policy response to COVID-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004190443/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/subjects/getting-help-during-coronavirus-covid-19/if-you-need-payment

C7_Notes: During this period, South Australia has implemented a hard border with ACT, NSW, Victoria and Queensland, as well as parts of the Northern Territory, thus prohibiting people from these regions to enter. There are exemptions for essential travellers and permitted arrivals, however, they must self quarantine for 14 days. People from Tasmania and Western Australia are permitted to enter without restriction as long as they have not been in a restricted zone in the past 14 days.   This is a minor tightening of restrictions, as previously travel from the whole of the NT was unrestricted. The overall policy of prohibiting entry to SA from high-risk regions remains unchanged.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210820011513/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/restrictions-and-responsibilities/travel-restrictions/sa-border-restrictions
H8_Notes: Current restrictions in South Australia do not allow visits to aged care facilities: - If you have a fever or symptoms of a respiratory infection such as a cough, sore throat or shortness of breath - If you have been directed by an authorised officer to quarantine - If you been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days or anyone with a high temperature, fever, chills, symptoms of acute respiratory infection, or loss of taste and smell, in the last 72 hours.  All people (excluding residents) at a Residential Aged Care Facility must wear a mask.  This is a continuation of prior restrictions since at least 15 July 2021 (the date the linked source was last updated)  https://web.archive.org/web/20210927202848/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/restrictions-and-responsibilities/visits-to-residential-care-facilities

C8_Notes: As noted by the Department of Home Affairs, between 18 August 2021 and 31 August 2021, foreign travellers are banned from entering Australia subject to limited exemptions. E1_Notes: On 16 September 2021, the COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week.   The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.   Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period. The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments

H8_Notes: According to The Emergency Management (Residential Aged Care Facilities No 43) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 which was implemented from 12:31 pm on 24 November 2021, individuals were prohibited from entering a residential aged care facility unless they were residents of the facility, worked at the facility (as an employee, contractor, student, or volunteer), were conducting a prospective resident visit, were providing essential goods or services (including legal, medical, emergency management, or regulatory services) for the facility or its residents, were conducting a care or support visit for a resident at the facility, or were participating in a group activity led by a worker from the facility.    The above individuals were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had COVID-19 symptoms, had contact with a known COVID-19 case without wearing PPE in the 14 days preceding entry, had not received the influenza vaccine since 1 June 2021 (unless they were observing the waiting period between the COVID-19 and influenza vaccines), were awaiting a COVID-19 test result (unless their COVID-19 test was for the purpose of routine monitoring of asymptomatic individuals), or were prohibited from entering due to an Arrivals direction (e.g. they had been in a high-risk area in the 14 days prior to entry). Masks were mandatory for workers and visitors in residential aged care facilities when in the presence of other persons.    The Emergency Management (Residential Aged Care Facilities No 43) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 also specified different regulations for care and support visits according to aged care facility vaccination rates. Residents of aged care facilities with a vaccination rate of less than 70% were only allowed to receive two care and support visits with one person OR one care and support visit with two people per day. Residents of aged care facilities with a vaccination rate of more than 70%, as well as residents receiving end of life support were not subjected to these visitor restrictions.    In addition to the new Direction, the 24 November 2021 version of the SA Government website stated that individuals could only enter aged care facilities if they had received all doses of an approved COVID-19 vaccine.  COVID-19 vaccines were highly recommended for aged care facility residents.    Aged care workers were only allowed to provide personal care at one residential aged care facility (if possible), and were not allowed to work at their aged care facility if they had worked in a medi-hotel in the past 14 days. They also had to complete COVID-19 training modules and wear PPE. All aged care facilities were required to submit workforce management and infection control plans.      The directions introduced on 24 November 2021 represented a tightening of previous COVID-19 restrictions to limit entry into aged care facilities, and the directions in place between 25 November 2021 and 2 December 2021 were a continuation of these restrictions. Due to the presence of vaccine-related restrictions H8 was coded as 3G, although it would be coded as 2G if allowances for vaccinated visitors and staff were taken into account. All activities, events, and gatherings attended by more than 1000 people, as well as licensed premises providing entertainment of a sexually explicit nature were required to have a COVID Management Plan. Activities, events, or gatherings with over 1000 attendees and multiple vendors were required to submit both a COVID Management Plan (for the event as a whole) and COVID-Safe plans (for individual vendors). C7_Notes: According to the SA Government EntryCheck webpage (as of 25 November 2021), all unvaccinated individuals were prohibited from entering the state unless they had successfully applied for an exemption. All individuals (regardless of vaccination status) travelling to SA from interstate or overseas was required to apply to do so through EntryCheck SA    Arrivals from 'very low risk' Australian jurisdictions with no evidence of COVID-19 community transmissions could enter South Australia if they were vaccinated.    Arrivals from 'low risk' Australian jurisdictions with evidence of COVID-19 community transmissions and a vaccination rate of 90% or higher (e.g. the ACT, NSW, and Victoria) were required to take a COVID-19 test within 72 hours prior to arrival in SA as well as complete a daily COVID-19 symptom check for 14 days after arrival.    Arrivals from 'moderate risk' Australian jurisdictions with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a vaccination rate of 80% or higher were required to do the following:  	- Take a COVID-19 test within 72 hours before arriving in SA, as well as within 24 hours after arrival in SA  	- Quarantine in SA until they had taken a COVID-19 test  	- Complete a daily COVID-19 symptom check for 14 days after arrival    Arrivals from 'high risk' Australian jurisdictions with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate of 80% or lower were required to do the following:  	- Obtain a negative COVID-19 test result in the 72 hours prior to arrival in SA  	- Quarantine for 7 days  	- Complete a COVID-19 test 24 hours, 6 days, and 13 days after arrival in SA  	- Complete a daily COVID-19 symptom check for 14 days after arrival  	- Refrain from entering high risk settings and COVID Management Plan events for 14 days after arrival    From the SA Government website as of 25 November 2021, fully vaccinated individuals from cross-border communities and unvaccinated cross-border community members aged between 12 years and 2 months and 18 years could apply to enter SA.  Cross-border community members were required to have a COVID-19 test within 24 hours of their arrival in SA if they had left the cross-border corridor on the NSW or Victorian side for more than 72 hours. There were no further restrictions on arrivals from 'very low risk' areas with no evidence of COVID-19 community transmissions (e.g. Queensland, Tasmania, and Western Australia).       Arrivals from 'low risk' areas with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate of 90% or higher (e.g. ACT and Victoria) were required to obtain a negative COVID-19 test result within 72 hours before arriving in SA, as well as undergo a daily symptom check for 14 days after arrival. Arrivals from 'high risk areas', or areas with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate less than 80% were required to do the following:  	- obtain a negative COVID-19 test result within 72 hours before arriving in SA  	- Quarantine for 7 days after arrival  	- Take COVID-19 tests 24 hours, 6 days, and 13 days after arrival  	- Undergo daily symptom checks and avoid high risk settings and COVID Management Plan events during the 14 days after arrival    Individuals who had close contact with a COVID-19 case within 7 days before arriving in SA were prohibited from entering the state. E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).    The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.    The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.    A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.    The directions in place between 30 January and 5 February 2022 were a continuation of existing directions. H7_Notes: According to the Australian Government Department of Health website (as last updated 3 February 2022), the Australian Government had been distributing COVID-19 vaccines through Operation COVID Shield, the national taskforce coordinating the Australian vaccine rollout.    As part of the rollout, all Australians* aged 5 years and over could book a free COVID-19 vaccination appointment, although it was slightly more difficult for those in the 5-11 year age group to receive a vaccine compared to other eligible age groups, as not all vaccine providers were able to provide the smaller Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose for 5-11 year olds.    The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.    As 93.65% of Australians aged 16 years and above had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, 77.11% of Australians aged 12-15 years old had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, and 44.15% of Australians aged 5-11 years old had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, the Australian Government was likely able to deliver on its universal vaccination policy. Nonetheless, State and Territory Governments also delivered their own updates and specialised services to meet the needs of their jurisdictions.
