H8_Notes: On 21 April (the continuation of the existing policy), the National Cabinet reconfirmed the principles announced on 18 March 2020 regarding visits to aged care facilities. In line with these principles, visits should be limited to a short duration, a maximum of two visitors at one time per day, and conducted in line with social distancing practices.   Infection prevention and control measures must be balanced against the needs and best interests of residents. Aged care providers are best placed to make these assessments on a case by case basis.    National Cabinet also reiterated that the following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter the aged care facilities:  â€¢	Those who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days;  â€¢	Those who have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days;  â€¢	Those with fever or any (even mild) symptoms of acute respiratory infection (e.g. cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath); and  â€¢	Those who have not been vaccinated against influenza (after 1 May).    https://web.archive.org/web/20220515000643/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures-210420    Additionally, on 24 April, the National government stressed that the AHPPC advice that it is not acceptable for any facility to put in place restrictions beyond the principles agreed on 17 March 2020. These include complete lockdowns or banning all visits from carers and families, other than during a specified facility outbreak.  Facilities need to know the appropriate levels of infection control and prevention to implement, in consultation with the relevant public health units and the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission. The Commonwealth Government will continue to monitor the situation and will take steps, if necessary, to require facilities to seek an exemption from the Commission before implementing additional restrictions.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220515000647/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures-24april20

H8_Notes: This is a continuation of the existing policy commenced in April. The national government agreed that visits in aged care facilities should be limited to a short duration, a maximum of two visitors at one time per day, and conducted in line with social distancing practices. Infection prevention and control measures must be balanced against the needs and best interests of residents. Aged care providers are best placed to make these assessments on a case by case basis. The following visitors and staff (including visiting workers) should not be permitted to enter the aged care facilities: â€¢ Those who have returned from overseas in the last 14 days; â€¢ Those who have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days; â€¢ Those with fever or any (even mild) symptoms of acute respiratory infection (e.g. cough, sore throat, runny nose, shortness of breath); and â€¢ Those who have not been vaccinated against influenza (after 1 May). The national government stressed that it is not acceptable for any facility to put in place restrictions beyond the principles agreed. These include complete lockdowns or banning all visits from carers and families, other than during a specified facility outbreak. Facilities need to know the appropriate levels of infection control and prevention to implement, in consultation with the relevant public health units and the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission. The Commonwealth Government will continue to monitor the situation and will take steps, if necessary, to require facilities to seek an exemption from the Commission before implementing additional restrictions. Additionally, on 1 May, the Morrison government announces the additional covid-19 specific support packaging totalling $205 million under targeted measures. The support is aimed at ensuring aged care providers can offer reinforced levels of safety and care for those who need it most. H8_Notes: Residential aged care facilities were legally responsible for infection prevention and control under the Aged Care Act 1997 and the Aged Care Quality Standards. In the COVID-19 Infection Prevention and Control for Residential Care Facilities updated on 17 May 2020, there were visitor restriction and signage:  â€¢ Ensure that all visitors, including essential external providers and visitors to residents:  o Visit only one resident (or essential staff member).  o Go directly to the residentâ€™s room or area designated by the Residential Care Facilities (RFC), and avoid communal areas.  o Maintain separation of 1.5 metres from residents, if possible.  o Use alcohol-based hand rub or wash their hands before entering and on leaving the RCF and the residentâ€™s room.  o Practice cough etiquette/respiratory hygiene.  o If visiting a resident who is in isolation or quarantine, observe contact and droplet precautions, as directed by RCF staff.  â€¢ Screen visitors on entry to the facility for epidemiological (recent travel, contact with a COVID-19 case) and clinical risk factors (acute respiratory infection).  Website about Providing aged care services during COVID-19: https://web.archive.org/web/20200618105452/https://www.health.gov.au/news/health-alerts/novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov-health-alert/coronavirus-covid-19-advice-for-the-health-and-aged-care-sector/providing-aged-care-services-during-covid-19  COVID-19 Infection Prevention and Control for Residential Care Facilities (MAY 16, 2020): https://web.archive.org/web/20200527204540/https://www.health.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2020/05/coronavirus-covid-19-guidelines-for-infection-prevention-and-control-in-residential-care-facilities_0.pdf

H8_Notes: As of January 2021, there are extensive restrictions on entry to aged care facilities, as outlined by the CHO's COVID-19 Directions (No. 40) 2020. Non-residents must not visit an aged care facility unless they:  -	work at the facility  -	are providing essential goods or services to the facility  -	are providing healthcare or medication to a resident  -	are providing care and support (including end-of-life support) to a resident  -	are present for emergency management or law enforcement  -	are a prospective resident  -	are providing legal services to residents  -	are performing regulatory functions (e.g. inspections).  Even if they belong to one of these permitted categories, people must not visit aged care facilities if they:  -	have been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case in the last 14 days  -	have a fever higher than 37.5 degrees, or symptoms of respiratory illness  -	are not vaccinated against the flu.   This is a continuation of policy since 24 June 2020, when Direction No. 40 took effect.    Source: http://web.archive.org/web/20210423081457/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/898953/cho-directions-no40-directions-aged-care-facilities.pdf

H8_Notes: On June 30 2021, Hugh Heggie, Chief Health Officer, announced in a COVID-19 Direction that from July 1 a person must not enter or remain on the premises of an aged care facility unless the person is one of the  following:  (a) an officer, employee or contractor of the facility;  (b) a person providing goods or services necessary for the operation  of the facility;  (c) a person providing health, medical or pharmaceutical goods or  services to a resident of the facility;  (d) a person providing end of life support to a resident of the facility;  (e) a person required for emergency management or law enforcement;  (f) a legal practitioner providing legal services regarding end of life  matters to a resident of the facility only if the service cannot be  provided remotely.  	  It also restricts people who have symptoms of COVID-19 or are unvaccinated from entering aged care facilities. However, aged care residents were not restricted from leaving the premises.   	  This represents a continuation of the policy response to COVID-19, as similar restrictions were announced on June 27 in response to lockdowns announced in Darwin and Alice Springs. This policy remained current on July 3-9.     https://web.archive.org/web/20211102035935/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0014/1020461/cho-directions-nr19-of-2021.pdf     https://web.archive.org/web/20210902045643/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0016/1019023/cho-directions-nr11-2021-directions-for-aged-care-facilities.pdf

E2_Notes: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. These Notices provide the framework for the Territoryâ€™s response to tenancy issues arising as a result of the COVID-19 emergency. The policies remained in effect as of July 2021, thus representing a continuation of policy sinec 2020.  The amendments increased the notice timeframes for Termination other than breaches of agreement to 60 days for both fixed term and periodic tenancy agreements (currently 14 days for fixed term agreements and 42 days for periodic tenancies). It also extended the length of time that rent has to be in arrears for termination for non-payment of rent where COVID 19 hardship is present to 60 days (originally 14 days of rent arrears). Unpaid rent is still owed to landlords.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211104045430/https://consumeraffairs.nt.gov.au/rental-changes-due-to-covid-19/overview-of-modifications-to-processes

E2_Notes: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. These Notices provide the framework for the Territoryâ€™s response to tenancy issues arising as a result of the COVID-19 emergency. The amendments increased the notice timeframes for Termination other than breaches of agreement to 60 days for both fixed term and periodic tenancy agreements (currently 14 days for fixed term agreements and 42 days for periodic tenancies). E1_Notes: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. H7_Notes: According to the Australian Government Department of Health website (as last updated 3 February 2022), the Australian Government had been distributing COVID-19 vaccines through Operation COVID Shield, the national taskforce coordinating the Australian vaccine rollout.    As part of the rollout, all Australians* aged 5 years and over could book a free COVID-19 vaccination appointment, although it was slightly more difficult for those in the 5-11 year age group to receive a vaccine compared to other eligible age groups, as not all vaccine providers were able to provide the smaller Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine dose for 5-11 year olds.    The Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine was available for individuals aged 5 years and above, the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals aged 60 years and above (or 18-59 year olds who had chosen to take the vaccine after consulting with a healthcare professional), and the Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine was available to individuals 12 years and above. The Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine was also available to those aged 18 years old and above after being provisionally approved by the TGA on 20 January 2022.    Booster vaccines were available for individuals aged 16 years and above who had completed their primary course of COVID-19 vaccination at least 3 months ago. 16-17 year olds could take the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine as part of their booster dose, and those aged 18 years and above could either take the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or the Pfizer COVID-19 for their booster shot.    Immunocompromised individuals could also take a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.    As 93.65% of Australians aged 16 years and above had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, 77.11% of Australians aged 12-15 years old had received two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine, and 44.15% of Australians aged 5-11 years old had received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, the Australian Government was likely able to deliver on its universal vaccination policy. Nonetheless, State and Territory Governments also delivered their own updates and specialised services to meet the needs of their jurisdictions. E2_Notes: The ACT Government implemented measures to support households as part of its economic survival package. These included:  -	Rebates to utility and residential rates bills  -	Additional rebates on rates and taxes for landlords who reduce their rents  -	Deferral of rates payments for homeowners suffering financial hardship because of COVID-19  -	Freezing of fees and levies (e.g. parking fees, vehicle registration fees, public transport fares, the fire/emergency services levy). H1_Notes: The ACT government has a dedicated website for the pandemic. It maintains a series of social media profiles, on which it posts information on the pandemic.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200813/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/home
H2_Notes: Anyone exhibiting symptoms of COVID, no matter how mild, is eligible for a test.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200813063943/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested
H3_Notes: The ACT government regularly publishes statistics on the pandemic such as daily cases, tests conducted, etc. The list of confirmed cases is constantly being updated.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200811005948/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates/confirmed-case-information
H6_Notes: Masks are not required in the ACT. The health advice remains that where there is no community transmission of COVID-19, masks are not required.   Exceptions include symptomatic/quarantining individuals who need to leave for an essential reason. People over 60 with underlying health problems and are unable to stay 1.5 metres away from others should wear a mask. Furthermore, people who have underlying health issues and are unable to stay 1.5 metres away from others should also use a mask.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200811005938/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/protect-yourself
H7_Notes: COVID-19 vaccines were not yet available at this time. The ACT's vaccination rollout began on February 22, 2021     https://web.archive.org/web/20210515021544/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/vaccine/when-will-i-get-the-covid-19-vaccine

C1_Notes: ACT public schools have returned to face-to-face instruction, with remote options available for students vulnerable to COVID-19. However, camps, interstate excursions, large gatherings of more than 100 people, discos and celebrations, and in-person fundraisers involving adults have been cancelled. Small scheduled events, such as one-on-one parent-teacher interviews and small assemblies of less than 100 people, may continue. Schools are instructed to keep records of all visitors to assist potential contact tracing.  This is a continuation of policy since July 2020; see https://web.archive.org/web/20220611110836/https://www.education.act.gov.au/about-us/all-news-and-news-alerts/news-items/july-2020/updated-information-on-covid-19-health-directions-and-restrictions-for-act-public-schools.
C2_Notes: The ACT moved to stage 3.1 of its recovery roadmap on 10 August 2020. Some additional categories of businesses (e.g. casinos, food courts, saunas, strip clubs, brothels, and 24-hour gyms) were allowed to reopen; following this easing of restrictions, only high-risk businesses (e.g. nightclubs) were required to remain closed. Non-essential businesses may host up to 100 people, provided that social distancing of 1 person per 4 square metres is maintained and a COVID-19 safety plan is followed. Employees are encouraged to work from home when this is possible. See https://web.archive.org/web/20210226110338/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0007/1610944/CV_Roadmap_Recovery-plan_Ease_Restrictions_20August20.pdf.
C3_Notes: Large events of more than 100 people are not permitted. Smaller events may continue provided that social distancing of 1 person per 4 square metres is maintained. For gatherings conducted at a "non-essential business or undertaking" (which includes religious services, weddings and funerals, conferences and conventions, public performances, sporting events and cinemas) event organisers are also required to follow a COVID-19 safety plan and keep records of attendees to assist contact tracing.   This is a continuation of previous policy since at least June 2020. See Phase 3.1 of the COVID-19 Recovery Plan: https://web.archive.org/web/20210627101158/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/1629330/PICC0050-COVID-Recovery-Plan.pdf   and Restricted Activities Direction No. 7: http://web.archive.org/web/20220622095330/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-484/20200812-74810/html/2020-484.html
C4_Notes: Gatherings are limited to 100 people, or 1 person per 4 square metres, whichever is lesser. Gatherings regarded to be essential (e.g. gatherings necessary for normal operations of a workplace, shopping centre, health care facility, airport, school, or legislative body; gatherings for emergency or law enforcement purposes; gatherings for the purpose of private or public transportation) are excepted from restrictions. This is a continuation of policy since at least 12 August 2020, see http://web.archive.org/web/20220622095330/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-484/20200812-74810/html/2020-484.html
C5_Notes: Public transport continues to operate and timetables are unchanged, but people are encouraged to use private transport if they can, and avoid public transport if they are feeling unwell.     A number of other precautionary measures have also been implemented:  -	Cash payments of fares are no longer accepted  -	Front seats of buses are closed off to ensure social distancing between passengers and the driver  -	Light rail doors open automatically, so passengers don't need to push the button  -	Additional hygiene measures (e.g. hand sanitizer for drivers, additional cleaning).  -	Passengers are advised to maintain social distancing, and travel outside peak hours.    See https://web.archive.org/web/20200901054233/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/transport.
C6_Notes: As of August 20, 2020, the ACT is in stage 3.1 of its roadmap to recovery (see https://web.archive.org/web/20210226110338/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0007/1610944/CV_Roadmap_Recovery-plan_Ease_Restrictions_20August20.pdf). Given that most non-essential businesses were permitted to open, it can be assumed there were no stay-at-home orders at this time.
C7_Notes: As of August 20, 2020, travellers from Victoria who are not residents in the ACT are not permitted to enter the ACT, unless they have been granted an exemption by ACT Health. ACT residents may return home from Victoria, but must quarantine for 14 days since they were last in Victoria. Travellers from elsewhere in Australia are not required to quarantine, but are advised to avoid high-risk settings if they have visited Greater Sydney or other COVID-19 affected areas. ACT residents are advised not to travel outside the ACT unless it is essential, but are not forbidden from doing so. This is a continuation of previous policy, aside from the recent removal of Newcastle from the list of COVID-19 affected areas.  See https://web.archive.org/web/20200826011420/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/travel.
C8_Notes: Most travellers from overseas are banned from entering Australia since March 2020 (see   https://web.archive.org/web/20210416125022/https://www.homeaffairs.gov.au/foi/files/2020/fa-200700310-document-released.PDF) however, this is a federal government policy, and quarantine for incoming travellers is the highest level of restrictions imposed by the ACT Government specifically.  The ACT requires all travellers arriving from overseas (except New Zealand) to quarantine for 14 to 24 days after arrival, unless they are diplomats (who are requested but not required to quarantine) or crew members on international flights (who may leave quarantine early to fly out of the ACT). This is a continuation of policy since at least 6 July 2020, see https://web.archive.org/web/20220425003632/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-374/20200706-74574/html/2020-374.html
E1_Notes: There was no broad income support available during this time period (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200828065940/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/business-and-work/economic-survival-package/families-and-households). However, in August 2020, the ACT Government announced the introduction of a Hardship Fund for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19 and meet certain eligibility criteria (e.g. not having access to paid sick leave, having less than $5000 in savings, and not already receiving support from the federal government). This fund was not yet available as of August 28, 2020. See https://web.archive.org/web/20200929124134/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0007/1621627/CV_Hardship-Isolation-Payment-Guidelines.pdf for details.
E2_Notes: A range of measures to protect tenants and landlords affected by COVID-19 were in place for six months beginning on 22 April 2020. This included a moratorium on evictions for tenants unable to pay rent as a result of COVID-19 impacts. Landlords are also prohibited from increasing rent for households impacted by COVID-19. See https://web.archive.org/web/20201023000436/https://www.justice.act.gov.au/safer-communities/protection-rights/information-tenants-and-occupants-impacted-covid-19
H1_Notes: The ACT Government runs a public information campaign through multiple channels. This campaign includes the ACT COVID-19 website (https://web.archive.org/web/20200827014244/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/) which publishes regular news updates, current restrictions and advice, information on available government support, and statistics of COVID-19 in the ACT.   ACT Health also operates a COVID-19 helpline over the phone (see archive link above) and is active on Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn and YouTube (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200925070057/https://health.act.gov.au/contact-us)
H2_Notes: ACT Health advises people to get tested if they have a fever of 37.5 degrees or higher, or have respiratory symptoms, while people with other symptoms may get tested after consulting with a doctor. Asymptomatic people are specifically instructed not to get tested, except in specific situations (e.g. for people in quarantine who may have been exposed to COVID-19, during outbreaks in aged care facilities and other high-risk settings, or for contact tracing purposes). See https://web.archive.org/web/20200820092154/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested
H3_Notes: There was no community transmission of COVID-19 at this time, so no contact tracing took place in practice. However, ACT Health contacts all confirmed COVID-19 cases to identify people they might have had contact with (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200820092154/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested) and publishes details of confirmed cases, including public transport that had passengers with COVID (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200819213042/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates/confirmed-case-information) indicating capacity for comprehensive contact tracing.  Non-essential businesses are also required to ensure visitors register their contact details to enable comprehensive manual contact tracing in the event of an outbreak. See http://web.archive.org/web/20220622095330/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-484/20200812-74810/html/2020-484.html
H6_Notes: There was no community transmission of COVID-19 in the ACT at this time, and healthy people were not required or recommended to wear masks. People are only advised to wear masks if they have COVID-19 symptoms and need to leave home for essential reasons, they are in quarantine and need to leave home for medical attention, or they are elderly/otherwise vulnerable. See http://web.archive.org/web/20200817070921/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/protect-yourself
H7_Notes: COVID-19 vaccines were not yet available at this time. The ACT's vaccination rollout began on February 22, 2021 (see https://web.archive.org/web/20210515021544/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/vaccine/when-will-i-get-the-covid-19-vaccine)
H8_Notes: As of 23 March 2020, people must not visit aged care facilities unless they are any of the following:  -	a resident, worker, or prospective resident at the facility  -	providing goods or services essential for the facility's operation  -	providing medical treatment to a resident  -	providing care or support (e.g. to a family member or close friend), including end-of-life support  -	there for emergency or law enforcement purposes    Even if they meet these requirements, people must not visit if they:  -	have been to Victoria, Greater Sydney, COVID-19 affected areas in Queensland, or anywhere outside Australia in the past 14 days  -	have been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case in the past 14 days  -	have a fever, recent history of fever, or respiratory symptoms  -	or have not been vaccinated against influenza.    See https://web.archive.org/web/20200821230540/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/aged-care

C3_Notes: During this time period, the ACT Easing of Restrictions Roadmap would have been at Phase 3.1 where although gatherings weren't forbidden, there was a 100 person cap limit (excluding on premise staff) and 1 person for every 4 square metres cap. C4_Notes: During this time period, per Phase 3.1 of the ACT government's COVID-19 Easing of Restrictions Roadmap, any gatherings held were capped at 100 people with 1 person per every 4 square meters. C5_Notes: During this time period, individuals are heavily recommended to only use public transport if they are feeling well. C6_Notes: During this time period, there were no mandates from the ACT government for individuals to remain at home unless they were infected by COVID-19 and were a close contact, where they had to self-isolate. Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200812202805/https://www.cmtedd.act.gov.au/open_government/inform/act_government_media_releases/barr/2020/further-restriction-easing-postponed-in-the-act (assume maintained until 3 September 2020)
C7_Notes: During this time period, there were restrictions with travel to NSW and Victoria from the ACT. Anyone other than ACT residents travelling to ACT from Victoria will not be allowed in unless granted an exemption by ACT Health. Anyone from COVID-affected areas is strongly discouraged from travelling to the ACT and be up to date with the most relevant public health alerts from their state. H2_Notes: During this time period, any individual who displayed symptoms of COVID-19 (involving fever of 37.5 degrees or higher and/or a respiratory infection) were suggested to take a COVID-19 test. H3_Notes: During this time period, contact tracing was regularly conducted in the ACT with case numbers frequently updated and anybody who was a close contact notified. This continues from previous policies.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200901054217/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates/confirmed-case-information
H7_Notes: During this time period, the vaccine was not yet considered available by the ACT government to any age group. This continues from previous policy.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200901054229/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/protect-yourself
H8_Notes: During this time period, the ACT government mandated that all individuals are not allowed to enter or remain on the premises of a residential aged care facilities unless:  -they are a resident  -they are an employee or contractor of the aged care facility  -person's presence is required for providing goods or services necessary for the operation of the facility  -person's presence is required for providing health, medical or pharmaceutical goods or services to a resident  -person's presence is for a care and support visit to a resident  -person's presence is for end of life support for resident  -they are prospective resident  -person's presence is required for emergency management or law enforcement    However, any person who has returned from overseas in the last 14 days, been in Victoria, Greater Sydney or COVID-affected areas of Queensland in the past 14 days, been in the contact of a confirmed COVID-19 case in the last 14 days, not have had 2020 influenza vaccine or has temperature higher than 37.5 degrees or symptoms of respiratory infection cannot enter aged care facilities at all.    No school or childcare groups are allowed to visit but children of all ages are allowed to, given they have received the 2020 influenza vaccine (exempting babies under 6 months) and follow restrictions during their visit. No more than two people can visit a resident at any time. These are considered extensive protections due to the heavy restrictions on individuals placed.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200901054307/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/aged-care

E2_Notes: A range of debt/contract relief has been provided by the ACT government for financially struggling individuals. First, the usual annual increase has not been applied to 2020-21 general rates bills and a $150 AUD ($110 USD) rebate has been provided to the fixed charge component of all general rates bills.    The Fire and Emergency Services Levy in 2020-21 has also been frozen at the 2019-20 level while the 2019-20 quarter 4 residential general instalments and land tax assessments has been delayed by 4 weeks and the 2020-21 quarter 1 residential general instalments and land tax assessments by 3 weeks.    Rates deferrals for owner occupiers experiencing hardship due to COVID-19 also can be deferred without interest for 12 months as long as income has been reduced by at least 25% due to unemployment, reduction in hours or loss of small business income. Land tax and rates rebates are also offered for landlords who reduce rent by at least 25% for tenants impacted by COVID-19 which is equal to 50% of rent reduction. Stamp duty concessions are also offered for some home buyers planning to live in their new property and households already receiving the Utilities Concession will receive an additional $200 AUD ($147 USD) rebate through their electricity bill. ACT Health also operates a COVID-19 helpline over the phone (see archive link above) and is active on Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn and YouTube (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200925070057/https://health.act.gov.au/contact-us)
H2_Notes: ACT Health advises people to get tested if they have a fever of 37.5 degrees or higher, or have respiratory symptoms, while people with other symptoms may get tested after consulting with a doctor. Asymptomatic people are specifically instructed not to get tested, except in specific situations (e.g. for people in quarantine who may have been exposed to COVID-19, during outbreaks in aged care facilities and other high-risk settings, or for contact tracing purposes). See https://web.archive.org/web/20200909171244/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested.
H3_Notes: There was no community transmission of COVID-19 at this time, so no contact tracing took place in practice. However, ACT Health contacts all confirmed COVID-19 cases to identify people they might have had contact with (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200909171244/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested) and publishes details of confirmed cases, including public transport that had passengers with COVID (see https://web.archive.org/web/20200901054217/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates/confirmed-case-information) indicating capacity for comprehensive contact tracing.  Non-essential businesses are also required to ensure visitors register their contact details to enable comprehensive manual contact tracing in the event of an outbreak. See http://web.archive.org/web/20220614004458/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-533/20200901-75020/html/2020-533.html
H7_Notes: COVID-19 vaccines were not yet available at this time. The ACT's vaccination rollout began on February 22, 2021 (see https://web.archive.org/web/20210515021544/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/vaccine/when-will-i-get-the-covid-19-vaccine)

C3_Notes: According to the Public Health (Restricted Activities â€“ Gatherings, Business or Undertakings) Emergency Direction 2020 (No 9) (ACT) (effective from 9 Sep 2020, 9:00 am to 17 Sep 2020), â€˜public eventsâ€™ were generally categorised as â€˜non-essential business or undertakingâ€™ in part 1 para 23. In part 1 para 3, a person who owns, controls or operates a non-essential business or undertaking in the ACT must comply with the requirements for a non-essential business or undertaking in this Direction.  This person must:  a.	develop and adhere to a COVID-19 Safety Plan, and produce the plan when requested by an authorised person; and  b.	display a sign specifying the maximum occupancy under this Direction of that business; and  c.	for contact tracing purposes, ask that each person who attends the business or undertaking record their attendance at the business or premises by either: (i) using the Check In CBR app; or (ii) providing a first name and contact phone number, and if provided, keep a record of those details, together with the date and time at which the person attended and produce the record if requested by an authorised person.    Each gathering (i.e. a group of 2 or more people occupying a single usable indoor space or usable outdoor space at the same time) in premises from where a non-essential business or undertaking operates must not exceed 1 person per 4 square metres or the maximum person limit (excluding a worker) per usable space in the premises (whichever is the lesser), subject to exceptions.    Part 1 para 23 sets out additional requirements for attending non-essential businesses or undertakings.    For example:  Gallery/museum (23(i))  -	the maximum person limit does not apply; and  -	if attending a tour, it cannot be more than 20 people, and the duration should be no more than 2 hours    It also suggested the followings (Attachment A):  -	In a given occupied space, there be a density of no more than 1 person per 4 square metres or the maximum person limit of usable space (whichever is the lesser), and this should take into account objects and items that may impact the total free space;  -	Hand hygiene products and suitable waste receptacles should be available, to allow for frequent cleaning and waste disposal;  -	Physical distancing of at least 1.5 metres between people, and physical contact should be avoided wherever possible;  -	The occupancy allowance should be displayed at the entrance of each venue or space;  -	The recommendations for unwell individuals to isolate at home and not attend published by the Commonwealth Department of Health should be promoted and displayed prominently so that they can be seen and read easily by a person at or near an entrance to the indoor space;  -	For settings where there is ongoing movement and an increased number of interactions between people (for example food markets) and an individualâ€™s attendance is not in the course of their employment at the place, an individualâ€™s attendance should be less than 2 hours duration;  -	Where activities involve the use of equipment, that equipment should be regularly cleaned and, where practicable, not be shared by people other than members of the same household.    This represents a 1G level of policy in the ACT as of 11 Sep 2020. C7_Notes: As of September 2020, travellers from Victoria who are not residents in the ACT are not permitted to enter the ACT, unless they have been granted an exemption by ACT Health. ACT residents may return home from Victoria, but must quarantine for 14 days since they were last in Victoria. Travellers from elsewhere in Australia are not required to quarantine, but are advised to avoid high-risk settings if they have visited COVID-19 affected areas in New South Wales or Queensland. ACT residents are advised not to travel outside the ACT unless it is essential, but are not forbidden from doing so. See https://web.archive.org/web/20200911081911/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/travel
C8_Notes: Most travellers from overseas are banned from entering Australia since March 2020     https://web.archive.org/web/20210416125022/https://www.homeaffairs.gov.au/foi/files/2020/fa-200700310-document-released.PDF    However, this is a federal government policy, and quarantine for incoming travellers is the highest level of restrictions imposed by the ACT Government specifically.    The ACT requires all travellers arriving from overseas (except New Zealand) to quarantine for 14 to 24 days after arrival, unless they are diplomats (who are requested but not required to quarantine) or crew members on international flights (who may leave quarantine early to fly out of the ACT).     This is a continuation of policy since at least 6 July 2020, see     https://web.archive.org/web/20220425003632/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-374/20200706-74574/html/2020-374.html

H8_Notes: During this time period, continuing from previous policy, various restrictions are placed on aged care facilities for the protection of the elderly. Individuals cannot enter or remain on the premises of an aged care facility unless the person is a resident, employee or contractor of the facility, the person's presence is required for purposes of providing essential goods or services for operation of the facility, providing health, medical or pharmaceutical goods or services to a resident, a care and support visit for resident, end of life support for resident, required for emergency management or law enforcement or the person is there as prospective resident of facility.     Only two visitors are allowed for a resident at any time although the number of hours is not restricted. The visit must be kept to a resident's room, outdoors or specific areas designated for visits. Physical distancing must also be practiced and any children must be supervised. However, if an individual has returned from overseas in past 14 days, been in Victoria, Greater Sydney or COVID-19 affected areas of Queensland in past 14 days, been in contact with confirmed COVID-19 case in past 14 days, have temperature higher than 37.5 degrees or history of fever or has symptoms of a respiratory infection or have not received 2020 flu vaccination and does not have a documented medical contraindication, they will not be allowed to enter the facility (whether as visitor or worker).    External excursions for groups of residents are not permitted, only to attend small family gatherings in line with government limits where a risk assessment should be conducted for each visit.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150903/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/aged-care

C1_Notes: Continuing from previous policy, all schools remain open during this time with most students and teachers having returned to school. However, some students who have chronic health conditions or compromised immune systems are still allowed to work or study from home. Large gatherings such as assemblies are slowly being reintroduced with various physical distancing and hygiene restrictions but the number of adults allowed into the school is still capped with records of visitors being kept to allow for contact tracing.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150845/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/students-education-childcare
C2_Notes: During this time period, the ACT was at Step 3.1 of the government's 'COVID-19 Easing of Restrictions Roadmap' where casinos and gaming in clubs, dine in food courts, steam based services, strip clubs and brothels and 24 hour gyms (max 25 people when unstaffed) were allowed to reopen. For these businesses, working from home was voluntary however, several sectors still at the time remained closed. From 18 September, smaller sized venues, facilities and businesses were allowed to return to pre-COVID capacity with maximum of 25 people (excluding staff) in the venue. All open businesses had to have a COVID-19 Safety Plan, a density limit of 1 person per 4 square metres and an absolute max of 100 people for each indoor and outdoor space.  Source:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210627101158/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/1629330/PICC0050-COVID-Recovery-Plan.pdf
C3_Notes: Under the 'Public Health (Restricted Activities - Gatherings, Business or Undertakings) Emergency Direction 2020 (No. 9)', various restrictions are placed on public gatherings for the event to be allowed to take place.    For non-essential events, a density limit of 1 person per 4 square meters is applied with a maximum limit of 100 people, a COVID-19 plan must be developed and adhered to and all people attending the business or undertaking must record their attendance through the Check in CBR app or a physical record.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20220621144648/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2020-592/20200909-75163/html/2020-592.html (active from 9 September 2020)
C4_Notes: During this time period, all public gatherings were restricted to at most 100 people with a density limit of one person per 4 square meters. There are, however, no limits with gatherings at home. Physical distancing of 1.5 meters and good hygiene is also recommended.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150901/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/groups-and-gatherings
C5_Notes: Individuals who are unwell or in quarantine or isolation are heavily suggested not to take public transport anywhere, instead using private transport. People in quarantine who need to ride public transport to get tested are allowed to use public transport as long as they wear a mask, sit at the back and maintain physical distance with other passengers. Public transport during this time doesn't accept cash, only MyWay or pre-purchased tickets and people are suggested to tap on and off to help wth contact tracing. Physical distancing and good hygiene practices is also emphasised.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150757/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/transport
C6_Notes: As seen in the ACT government's 'Canberra Recovery Plan: Easing of Restrictions', during this time period, public gatherings were allowed to occur and businesses were allowed to reopen. Thus, there were no particular requirements for individuals to stay at home, barr if they were found as a close contact or case.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150833/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/canberra-recovery
E2_Notes: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150838/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/business-and-work/economic-survival-package/families-and-households
H1_Notes: During this time period, the Canberran government continues to maintain a coordinated public campaign against COVID-19 with a regularly updated website containing daily case numbers, updates on health policy from the government and various advice on how to protect oneself against COVID-19. A COVID-19 helpline is also available to call from 8am-8pm daily as well as a variety of social media accounts with regular posts.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918152527/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/
H2_Notes: During this time period, continuing from previous policy, getting tested for COVID-19 was suggested for all individuals displaying a fever over 37.5 degrees or a respiratory infection, such as a sore throat or cough. Other circumstances might also cause individuals to be recommended for testing, including for people in quarantine who might have been exposed to COVID-19, during outbreaks in high-risk facilities or as part of public health investigations.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150803/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested
H3_Notes: During this time period, the ACT government continues to have comprehensive contact tracing with continuous updates to any cases of COVID-19 occurring on public transport or flights for the public to know as well as daily case numbers. Also, starting in September, the Check In CBR app has been made available to the general public allowing individuals to sign in whenever they enter a venue. The places any confirmed case visits is thus recorded and used to notify of any potential contacts.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200919094300/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates/confirmed-case-information  https://web.archive.org/web/20201205171352/https://www.act.gov.au/our-canberra/latest-news/2020/september/check-out-the-new-check-in-cbr-app
H6_Notes: During this time period, although masks were not required to be worn by the ACT government, they were recommended as a line of protection against COVID-19 along with physical distancing and good hygiene. Exceptions to this include having COVID-19 symptoms such as coughing and needing to leave home for an essential reason (e.g. getting tested, shopping for essential items), in quarantine or self-isolation and need to leave home for medical attention or have underlying health issues and cannot stay 1.5 meters from others.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150820/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/protect-yourself
H7_Notes: During this time period, no COVID-19 vaccines had yet been approved by the Canberran government for public use and thus a vaccination policy didn't exist. The earliest mention of vaccines being approved for use came in mid-January 2021 where a vaccination strategy program was due to start being implemented from mid-late February 2021.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20210119003350/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/covid-19-vaccine

C1_Notes: ACT public schools (Primary schools, high schools, and colleges) are open. Most students and teachers have returned to school. Students and teachers with chronic health conditions or compromised immune systems can work or study from home.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200929/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/students-education-childcare
C2_Notes: Most businesses are allowed to operate with certain restrictions. Businesses such as nightclubs are not yet allowed to operate. Venues, including food courts, must have a COVID Safety Plan. All venues must clearly display occupancy allowance at the entrance to each venue as well as display additional signs with area occupancy for separate individual spaces.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200803181222/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/what-you-can-do/faqs-changes-to-restrictions/summary-of-key-changes  https://web.archive.org/web/20200803174651/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/canberra-recovery
C3_Notes: Events are allowed; however, social distancing and good hygiene practices are mandatory. Indoor spaces must be large enough to allow for one person for every 4 square metres of space.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200803181222/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/what-you-can-do/faqs-changes-to-restrictions/summary-of-key-changes
C4_Notes: All public gatherings (except for the hospitality sector) will be set at one person per 4 square metres for each indoor and outdoor space, up to a maximum of 100 people (including staff, trainers and spectators).  https://web.archive.org/web/20200803181222/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/what-you-can-do/faqs-changes-to-restrictions/summary-of-key-changes
C5_Notes: People are encouraged to only use public transport when necessary and healthy. People who are in quarantine who need testing, or people who are symptomatic, can use public transport, rideshare or taxi to get to a testing centre, as long as they take appropriate precautions. There are currently no changes to timetables, but services are operating a bit differently to keep everyone safe. For instance: mandatory cashless payments.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200918150757/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/transport
C6_Notes: Under step 3.1 of Canberra's recovery plan, there are no stay-at-home requirements.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200929073500/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/canberra-recovery
C7_Notes: As of September 2020, travellers from Victoria who are not residents in the ACT are not permitted to enter the ACT, unless they have been granted an exemption by ACT Health. ACT residents may return home from Victoria, but must quarantine for 14 days since they were last in Victoria. Travellers from elsewhere in Australia are not required to quarantine, but are advised to avoid high-risk settings if they have visited COVID-19 affected areas in New South Wales or Queensland. ACT residents are advised not to travel outside the ACT unless it is essential, but are not forbidden from doing so. See https://web.archive.org/web/20200924022250/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/travel
H1_Notes: The ACT government has a website dedicated to the pandemic and has multiple social media profiles.   https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031522/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/home
H2_Notes: Anyone exhibiting symptoms of COVID is automatically eligible for a test.   https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031448/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested
H3_Notes: The ACT government regularly publishes updates on cases, possible sites of exposure as well as daily statistics on pandemic.   https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031545/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates  https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031522/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/home  https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031627/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/updates/confirmed-case-information
H6_Notes: While there is currently no community transmission of COVID-19 in the ACT, the ACT Government is still recommending people prepare for a time when face masks may become more routinely recommended. ACT residents - particularly those unable to physically distance in their work or daily activities - are encouraged to prepare for a time where masks are required. This includes work in customer-facing roles in hospitality or retail, public transport and places of worship, and may involve sourcing masks in preparation.   https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031502/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/protect-yourself
H8_Notes: Visits to aged care facilities are allowed if they are for the purposes of providing care and support. The duration is not limited. However, people cannot visit aged care facilities if they:  have returned from overseas in the last 14 days;  have been in Victoria and, specific local government areas of greater Sydney in the last 14 days;  have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days;  have a temperature higher than 37.5 degrees or history of fever (e.g. night sweats or chills) or symptoms of a respiratory infection such as a cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, loss of smell or loss of taste; or  have not had their 2020 influenza (flu) vaccination, unless they have a documented medical contraindication to receiving the vaccination.  https://web.archive.org/web/20201002031628/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/aged-care

C1_Notes: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser. The directions in place between April and May 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions. C1_Notes: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited.    The directions in place between April and May 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions. C2_Notes: According to the ACT Government website (as last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart.    The directions in place between 8 and 21 May 2021 were a continuation of existing directions. E2_Notes: The ACT introduced a range of actions and providing practical support, such as rebates and the freezing of some government fees to reduce pressure on household budgets.  Residential rates - The usual annual increase will not be applied to 2020-21 general rates bills. This combined with a $150 rebate to the fixed charge component of all 2020-21 residential rates bills means average residential general rates will not increase. Rates will reduce for around two-thirds of homeowners. Some homeowners will notice an increase due to their land value going up.  The government has also frozen the Fire and Emergency Services Levy in 2020-21 at the current 2019-20 level. C1_Notes: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported. Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited.    The directions in place during 15-27 June 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions. All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. C1_Notes: According to the Public Health (Mandatory Face Masks) Emergency Direction 2021, the ACT Government imposed a mask mandate which required individuals aged 12 years old and above to carry and wear a face mask in or at any business or undertaking. This mandate came into effect at 11:59pm on 27 July 2021, and was a tightening of existing COVID-19 restrictions.    All other directions pertaining to schools remained the same:    According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited. C2_Notes: According to the Public Health (Mandatory Face Masks) Emergency Direction 2021, the ACT Government imposed a mask mandate which required individuals aged 12 years old and above to carry and wear a face mask in or at any business or undertaking. This mandate came into effect at 11:59pm on 27 July 2021, and was a tightening of existing COVID-19 restrictions.    All other directions pertaining to businesses the same:    According to the ACT Government website (as of 27 June 2021 and last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart. C2_Notes: All non-essential businesses must follow a COVID-19 safety plan. In addition, most businesses are subject to a gathering limit of up to 25 people, and a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Some venues are exempt from the 25-person limit (e.g. cinemas, concert venues, stadiums, and convention centres) but may still be subject to the maximum density restrictions or other restrictions (e.g. only up to 75% capacity). C3_Notes: Event organisers are required to follow COVID Safe Event Protocols which states as follow:  - Events with 500 people or less can be organised without an exemption.  - Events between 501 and 1,000 people should notify ACT Health and submit COVID Safety Plan.  - Exemptions are required for events of more than 1,000 people.  - Events more than 10,000 are not considered for exemption. C4_Notes: Gathering sizes at most non-essential businesses are limited to 25 people, and in addition there is a maximum density of 1 person per 2 square metres. Some venues, such as concert halls, cinemas, stadiums, and convention centres, are exempt from the 25-person limit, but may still be subject to other restrictions (e.g. maximum density, or 75% capacity limit).   Major public events are also exempt from gathering caps, but must follow the COVID-19 Safe Event Protocols (see https://web.archive.org/web/20210725143420/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/1628637/PICC0032-ACT-COVID-Safe-events-protocol_v15.pdf):  -	Events of 500 people or less must follow 1 person/2 sq m rule and use the Check-In CBR app  -	Events of 500-1000 people must follow a COVID-19 safety plan, density limits (1 person/2 sqm) and use the Check-In CBR app.  -	Events of more than 1,000 people must also have an exemption from the Chief Health Officer.    This is a continuation of policy since 1 July 2021. See http://web.archive.org/web/20220730031350/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/View/ni/2021-405/20210701-77035/PDF/2021-405.PDF

E1_Notes: The COVID-19 Test Hardship Isolation Payment (worth $270) is available for ACT residents (or people who work in the ACT) who are isolating while waiting for a test result; cannot earn any income because they can't work; have no access to paid sick leave; have less than $5,000 in savings; and who aren't receiving Australian Government income support. E2_Notes: The ACT government has implemented a broad range of debt and contract relief measures to assist those experiencing hardship due to COVID-19.   -	Residential general rates bills were frozen for 2020-21, and did not increase as they did in previous years. Rebates of $150 were also applied to all 2020-21 rates bills.   -	The Fire and Emergency Services levy was also frozen at 2019-20 levels for 2020-21.  -	Rates deferrals available for homeowners experiencing significantly reduced income.  -	Land tax and rates rebates, worth half the rent reduction amount, for landlords who reduce rent by 25% or more.  -	Reduction or elimination of stamp duty for home buyers who plan on living in their new house.  -	Other government fees and charges, e.g. vehicle registration, parking, public transport, frozen at current levels.  -	A fund to help COVID-19-impacted households pay their utility bills. In continuation with existing policy schools and universities are back to on campus learning in the ACT.     The COVID Management Plan outlines basic public health measures in the following areas to reduce the spread of COVID-19:    - Eligible students (5 years and over) are strongly encouraged to be up-to-date with COVID-19 vaccinations.  - Check in is not required by staff or visitors  - Physical distancing should be maintained, but there are no density limits   - Students, staff and visitors with COVID-19 symptoms should not come to school  - Masks are not required except for staff when 1.5m distance cannot be maintained  - Cleaning  - Hand and respiratory hygiene  - Ventilation   - Testing 'as needed'  - Additional measures where there are a high number of COVID-19 exposures (additional staff testing, masks for some groups, limiting parents and carers on site, cancelling activities, cohorting, remote learning).  - International excursions are not permitted.  - Anyone who has attended a school while positive is required to notify the school. On confirmation of someone with COVID-19 (student, staff member, visitor) attending the school during their infectious period, the school will notify those impacted by a potential exposure (and their parent/carer). H8_Notes: As of 1 July 2022 these are continuing from June 3 2022,     There are no public health mandated visitor restrictions for ACT residential aged care facilities. Face masks are currently mandatory for staff and visitors aged 12 years and over.  People who are household or high risk contact of a COVID-19 case must not visit high-risk settings for 7 days after the last date of exposure or the last time someone tested positive in their household unless they are attending for urgent medical care.  From day 8 to 14 they are advised to limit their entry to high-risk settings unless prior approval has been granted by the facility, or if attending for urgent medical care.    Visits should not be in any inside communal areas.    Visits should be either in the residentâ€™s room or an outside area.    Entry screening  When visiting an aged care facility, you will be asked a set of screening questions on entry.  If you answer yes to any of the screening questions you will not be able to enter the facility.  The screening questions are subject to change depending on the COVID-19 situation, so it is important to check these regularly prior to visiting an aged care facility.  Visitors are encouraged to remember COVID Smart behaviours.  Visitors are strongly recommended to have the yearly influenza (flu) vaccine.    Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20220610075942/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/services-and-support/aged-care/advice-for-visitors-to-aged-care-facilities

V2_Notes: No changes to availbility    30 September 2022    After more than two and a half years, the ACTâ€™s Public Health Emergency Declaration has been revoked and the Government has transitioned the Territoryâ€™s public health response to COVID-19 to a COVID-19 Management Declaration and associated Directions.    The COVID-19 Management Declaration recognises the need to provide ongoing surveillance and management of the virus as we continue to transition to living with COVID-19.    Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the ACT community had responded incredibly well in its fight against COVID-19 since the public health emergency was declared in March 2020.    'This is the next stage in our COVID-19 response.There will need to be ongoing support for Canberrans who are most vulnerable to COVID-19, and a mechanism that allows the Government to swiftly implement the public health measures that have proven to be highly successful in suppressing the virus in the Territory,' Chief Minister Barr said.    Minister for Health Rachel Stephen-Smith said that some public health measures will remain to help ensure we continue to protect those in our community who are most at risk of severe health outcomes from COVID-19.    'The new COVID-19 settings are part of our staged plan to managing COVID-19 in a similar way to other infectious diseases like influenza,' Minister Stephen-Smith said.    'Canberrans should be reassured that if there is any significant development in relation to COVID-19, we will continue to take appropriate actions to keep our community safe, just as we have throughout the pandemic.'    Changes that came into effect today include:    Face masks no longer need to be worn on public and shared transport such as buses, light rail, taxis and ride share. ACT Health continues to recommend people wear a mask if it isnâ€™t possible to physically distance.  Household contacts no longer need to report their status to ACT Health.  COVID safety plans are no longer required for Canberra businesses and events. Planning tools will remain available, and ACT Health recommends businesses maintain an up to date COVID-19 safety plan to help manage the risk for staff, visitors and customers.  Vaccine mandates will no longer apply for workers in aged care facilities or disability care settings. Employers will now need to consider whether they wish to implement their own vaccination requirements in their employment policy or work health and safety settings.  Changes are also being made to COVID-19 testing arrangements in the ACT.    The Kambah COVID-19 drive through testing centre will permanently close at 4pm today (Friday 30 September) and the operating hours at the ACTâ€™s remaining testing centres will be reduced from tomorrow (Saturday 1 October).    As the COVID-19 response focuses on protecting and supporting those most at risk from severe illness from COVID-19, PCR testing will be prioritised for these groups.    RATs are readily available for anyone else with symptoms of COVID-19 as well as for asymptomatic individuals at ACT libraries.    Canberrans must continue to report positive rapid antigen tests (RATs) to ACT Health as soon as possible.    'I would encourage anyone needing a test to check the ACT COVID-19 website to confirm COVID-19 testing locations, opening hours and testing advice before they head to a testing centre,' Minister Stephen-Smith said.    If people have any COVID-19 symptoms, they should get tested for COVID-19 and stay at home.    The COVID-19 Management Declaration comes into effect under changes to the Public Health Act, that came into effect earlier this year.

Individuals are encouraged to stay in their known social groups and minimise the size of gatherings where possible.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220912200806/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
C5_Notes: Public transport services are operating as normal and mask-wearing on public transport is required.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220912200806/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
C6_Notes: There are no stay at home requirements. This is a continuation of the previous policy.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220901055656/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/quarantine
C7_Notes: There are currently no restrictions on interstate travel to the ACT. Persons who are currently under quarantine or isolation requirements seeking to travel to the ACT should refer to the entering and leaving the ACT page for further information.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220912200806/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
C8_Notes: There are currently no direct international flights arriving in the ACT. There are no quarantine or testing requirements for international travellers. All travellers can travel on to the ACT where permitted by their port of entry. International travellers should monitor for COVID-19 symptoms following their arrival into the ACT. If respiratory symptoms develop, stay home and get tested for COVID-19. Even if your test result is negative for COVID-19, you should stay home and minimise contact with others until you feel much better.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220828220021/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/travel/overseas-travel
E1_Notes: The COVID-19 Hardship Payment closed on 14 October 2022. (However, the scheme remains open to applicants who work in High Risk settings and are unable to attend work.)   https://web.archive.org/web/20221021011931/https://www.act.gov.au/business/business-support/covid-19-economic-support-for-business#Income%20support%20programs%20for%20workers
E2_Notes: There is no debt relief (eviction moratorium and post moratorium transitional support measures) for households, this has ended on 11 May 2022.   https://web.archive.org/web/20221017194556/https://www.justice.act.gov.au/renting-and-occupancy-laws/information-tenants-and-occupants
H1_Notes: The ACT government continue to provide important COVID-19 information and updates through their dedicated COVID-19 website.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220928143910/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/home
H2_Notes: It is advised that you get tested if you: -have any COVID-19 symptoms -are a household or high risk contact of a person diagnosed with COVID-19 -are travelling overseas and it is a requirement (see Capital Pathology, Laverty and Clinical Labs for more information)  Testing is not recommended within the first 28 days after you've been released from isolation as a positive case, unless you have symptoms and been specifically advised by your doctor to have a COVID-19 test.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220828220832/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/symptoms-and-getting-tested/when-to-get-tested
H3_Notes: The use of the Check In CBR app is no longer mandatory within the ACT. This is a continuation of the previous policy.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220706064555/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/check-in-cbr-app/information-for-customers
H6_Notes: A person aged 12 years or older must wear a face mask in certain settings. A person is not required to wear a face mask if they have a physical or mental health illness or condition, or disability, which makes wearing a face mask detrimental to their condition. This is a continuation of the previous policy.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220912200806/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
H7_Notes: Anyone aged 5 and above is eligible for a free Covid-19 vaccination.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220828221446/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/vaccine/when-will-i-get-the-covid-19-vaccine
H8_Notes: Visitors to comply with policies established by the relevant residential aged care facility. This is a continuation of policy across the state.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220813061842/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
